Question: How can we cut/build a square tiny layer cake?
Answer: People have been doing it for years. Any decent French bakery will have an array of decorated petit fours, and Italian bakeries have those cookies with jam between each brightly colored layer. Bake a thin sheet of the sponge of your choice, cut it into several pieces, and layer them with the filling of your choice. Watch it closely, as thin layers will bake quickly. You can also bake your sponge in cupcake molds, then slice it in layers, but the first method is easier. Warm jam is easy to spread in thin layers, but you might want buttercream or ganache. Up to you. It's easiest to do this step in larger format, then trim the individual cakes to the size you want. Dip them in ganache or royal icing, add a decorative touch or two, and you have your little cake. You could cut out tiny squares, if you wanted to be extra fussy, but working that size makes it very difficult to assemble neatly.

Question: Is a cupcake a muffin with icing?
Answer: Not exactly. Cupcakes are made with cake batter and almost always frosted. Muffin batter is leaner than cake batter and less sweet, or it ought to be. Muffins are also made with more inclusions, things like nuts, berries, chocolate chips and the like. As a general rule, muffins are quickbreads and the process of making them is different. So different in fact, that there is a whole class of baked goods where the simple instruction, “muffin method,” tells you everything you need to know. Combine the dry ingredients, combine the wet ingredients, combine the two, stirring as little as possible to avoid developing gluten. Many cupcakes on the other hand, use what is called the creaming method, in which sugar and butter are creamed together until soft and fluffy, eggs are added, then the dry ingredients and milk or other dairy. If you aren't a baker this doesn't seem very important, but it makes a big difference in the texture of the final product. Most cupcake recipes include more fat and sugar than most muffin recipes. A lot of muffins you find these days are very cakey, because people want to think they're eating something healthy, but they also want that added sweetness and fluffier texture. But traditionally, muffins and cupcakes are not at all the same.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: In YouTube videos I saw that the chef uses vanilla extract for making chocolate glaze but can I use chocolate extract for my chocolate glaze for donut?
Answer: The point of using vanilla extract in a chocolate glaze is to complement, rather than intensify the chocolate flavor. Using a chocolate extract will make the glaze more chocolatey. Using vanilla or one of the other flavors frequently paired with chocolate will make the glaze richer and more interesting. Some of the things aside from vanilla that are frequently paired with chocolate include coffee, cinnamon, orange, even a hint of cayenne. The additional flavors arent meant to stand out in the dish, just add a subtle note that boosts the chocolate in different ways. If you just want an intensely chocolate flavor there's no readon not to use chocolate extract, as long as it doesn't taste artificial. But you can also experiment with other flavors and see what they add to the mix.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Do vegans have an appreciation for carnivorous culinary skills?
Answer: Carnivores don't cook their food, so it's doubtful. I suppose that as vegans, most would appreciate the fact that animals need to eat, and have evolved to survive on a particular diet. Some vegans seem to think they can force carnivores to adapt, which explains the urge to turn dogs and cats into vegans, which is very unhealthy for the animals, to the point of blindness and death for cats. If you're asking as an omnivore if vegans can appreciate your cooking skills on an objective basis, sure- why not? They might not want to eat your boeuf Bourguignon or a perfectly roasted chicken, but if you made a nice, dairy free green bean casserole I'm sure they would enjoy it. Plenty of the food we eat as omnivores is slready vegan or can be easily adapted to suit vegan dietary requirements. The fact that you cared enough to take the trouble will always be appreciated. In fact, making tasty vegan food can be more of a challenge, which gives you a chance to show off your much vaunted culinary skills.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What caused my bread to smell bad after 3 days?
Answer: I have no idea, because you haven't told us enough about your bread. The first thing that comes to mind is that you haven't baked it to the proper temperature, had too much moisture left in the dough, and that encouraged mold and bacteria to take up residence. Bread needs to be baked to an internal temperature of at least 190°F/88°C. There are certainly other things that could cause your bread to smell off, but without more info, this is the most likely scenario.

Question: Which brand of bread flour can produce the most open crumb sourdough bread?
Answer: The brand of flour matters less than the protein content and the hydration of the dough. You want a bread flour (strong flour) that is somewhere between 12.5% and 14% protein. Which brands are available in your location may differ, but checking protein content is a reliable indicator. Hydration (percentage of water to flour) is another key to open crumb dourdough, usually at fairly high hydration. Somewhere around 75% to 80% is standard, and if you're making ciabatta it can be as high as 85% - 90%. How you handle, shape, and bake the bread also makes a difference. The best site I've found to explore the process of baking with sourdough is Foodgeek. Foodgeek He experiments with different methods of fermenting, kneading, shaping and proofing bread, with good explanations of why he does what he does. It's worth checking out the channel if you want to learn more.

Question: Is there a difference between Pickles and Pickled Cucumbers? I know that pickles are made of cucumbers, but do the cucumbers have to be pickled for a specific amount of time before they can be considered pickles?
Answer: Anything can be pickled. Pickling is a process, not an end result. Cucumbers are a particular favorite in western cuisine, but look to Japan or India and you will find an astonishing array of pickled vegetables made in different ways with all kinds of flavors from hot to salty to sweet. Even in countries where pickled cucumbers are common, you find all kinds of other pickled stuff. Pickled eggs, pickled beets, pickled beans, pickled ham hocks, pickled peaches (yum!), pickled walnuts, pickled watermelon rind, pickled relishes and chutneys, The well known Branston Pickle, a mixture of swedes (rutabagas), carrots, onions, cauliflower in a sweet and tangy combination of vinegar and dates, among other flavors, is just one example of that. Pickling is one of many ways to preserve food. You can submerge the food in salt or brine and lacto-ferment it, or you can make a pickling solution with vinegar, salt, sugar, and spices. Go further afield and you will find foods pickled in miso and in rice. Pickles of all sorts are an important part of global cuisine, because before refrigeration people had to find ways to preserve their harvest. Saurkraut is pickled cabbage. So is kimchi, though there are lots of varieties of kimchi that don't use cabbage. Pickled cucumbers are just cucumbers that have been pickled. But really, a pickle can be anything, as long as it has been fermented in some sort of brine. As for how long it takes before something can be called a pickle, you can make quick pickles in an hour, if you slice them thin enough. Cucumber chips, sure, but you can pickle radishes, onions, zucchini, all kinds of veggies this way. Slice your vegetables as thinly as possible and add them to a bowl. In a saucepan bring a cup of vinegar and half a cup of water to a boil. Add a tablespoon of kosher salt and a tablespoon of sugar, plus some pickling spices (bay leaves, coriander, black peppercorns, cinnamon, mace) and let the spices steep for 15-20 minutes before straining and pouring over the veggies. Cover and let sit in your fridge for an hour and you will have pickles. Add some chili flakes if you like them hot, or more sugar if you prefer them sweet. Toss in a whole garlic clove if you like garlic. These things are great in salads, in sandwiches, or just as a tasty side dish, and they'll keep for a couple of weeks in the fridge.

Question: How do you make rolls from scratch without yeast?
Answer: Without yeast? You can't make rolls because rolls are made with yeasted dough. But you do have a few options. You can make biscuits (American style) using baking powder, butter, and buttermilk. Light, flaky, and delicious, when done right. You could make popovers, though they can be a bit tricky. An eggy batter added to a very hot popover pan. The heat encourages a good rise, and you get a tall, semi-hollow popover. Cheesy ones make nice accompaniments tor roast meat. Popover batter is almost the same as that used for Yorkshire puddings, so you could also make those. The last option is some kind of quickbread baked in muffin cups. Cornbread, perhaps. You can leave it plain, add sugar if you prefer it sweet, or add fresh corn and diced jalapenos gor an interesting variation. Non of these will have the same flavor or texture as a nice dinner roll made with a yeasted dough, but they are all easy, tasty choices.

Question: Should you boil a potato to soften it before baking it to make a baked potato?
Answer: I wouldn't bother. I do stick a metal skewer lengthwise through the potato, which transfers heat into the center and helps it cook faster. I learned that trick from my mom, who came home from work and had to get dinner on the table.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Can we add wholewheat flour to all-purpose flour (both in equal parts) for pizza dough? Because pizza flour is not readily available and I always make pizza with all purpose flour but was thinking to add wholewheat flour too today; is it bad to do?
Answer: There's nothing wrong with adding some whole wheat flour to your pizza dough. It will change the texture and taste a little, but that can be a good thing. If you can get bread flour instead of all purpose, that will make a better pizza crust, and you can add about 30% whole wheat flour without compromising the texture. The only problem I can imagine is that the dough will need a bit of added gluten if you want a stretchy, thin crust style dough. Whole grain flours tend to make dough less extensible. You can add a tablespoon or two of vital wheat gluten to the next batch if you find that's an issue.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What is the weirdest thing you have seen pickled that was surprisingly delicious?
Answer: The oddest pickles I've had were probably the kudzu stalks a friend of mine brought to a party. Kudzu is mostly known as an incredibly invasive weed in the southern US, where it smothers trees, engulfs wrecked buses and abandoned homes, and generally runs rampant. But the entire plant is edible, even the fuzzy leaves. They're best if blanched to remove the fuzz, and can be added to salads, sauteed with bacon, or stuffed like cabbage leaves. The tender stalks were surprisingly tasty, a bit like pickled green beans. Fortunately, kudzu doesn't grow up here in western NY, but if it did I'd be making pickles in the spring.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What is special about Dole mini-bananas, other than the size novelty?
Answer: I suspect that along with the novelty of size, Dole is exploring the potential replacements for Cavendish bananas. The big yellow bananas we're all so used to in stores are in serious trouble around the globe. Since they are propagated by cloning, they are susceptible to disease, and are threatened by the spread of a strain of Fusarium fungus, also known as Panama Disease or Tropical Race 4 (TR4). The Cavendish bananas were actually a replacement for the formerly popular Gros Michel bananas, which also succumbed to a similar fungus in the 1940s. Dole may be looking to market new varieties of bananas that are less susceptible to the disease. In addition to baby bananas, I've also been seeing the smaller red-skinned bananas in stores, which are also tastier than the Cavendish.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: I'm planning on using ink as an art medium. What ink/pen should I start with?
Answer: The possibilities aren't exactly endless, but they are varied enough that you'll be spoiled for choice. Ink as a medium can be anything from a ball point pen to a dip pen and a bottle of ink. In between you have gel pens, any number of art markers, brush pens, even markers with calligraphy nibs. I've used dozens of different pens over the years, and they all have different things to recommend them. My advice is to start simply, with a few pens you think might be interesting. I like a medium point fountain pen with a flexible nib, but you may find other pens suit your personal style. Making art is about finding things you enjoy working with, then learning to use them to the best effect. And that takes some experimentation. Most good art supply stores are set up so you can test pens before you buy them, so do that. See if you like a fine point or something heavier, a variable line or a consistent one, a deep, rich black ink or something like grey or sepia. In the end, it's about finding something that works for you, that brings you joy. My tree made with gel pens on cardstock as part of the Lockdown Diorama.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What kinds of greens from the garden can you eat that we don't usually use? Can you eat potato, carrot, and radish tops? What else in the garden can you eat that you usually throw away?
Answer: I've seen recipes for pesto made with carrot tops. The one time I tried it was disappointing. They just don't have a lot of flavor. On the other hand, radish greens are wonderful in salads, as are young beet greens. Pea shoots are delicate and tender, and garlic scapes, the curly green shoots that spring from the bulbs in the late spring (depending on your planting zone), are delicious. There are also flowers that make good eating, like squash and lily blossoms, but you need to be cateful with lilies, because they arent all edible. Potato leaves are not recommended, since the grern parts of the plant are mildly to seriously toxic and can make you quite ill. It's fun to explore what some people call root to shoot eating, but it's a good idea to check a reliable reference before eating things you aren't familiar with.

Question: What's wrong with loving pumpkin spice pie over sweet potato? I love pumpkin spice pie!
Answer: To start with, it isn't pumpkin spice pie, it's just pumpkin pie. Pumpkin spice is something invented by food manufacturers and chain retaurants, to get people to buy more stuff. Every good baker has their own particular combination of warm spices they add to pumpkin pies. The usual suspects include things like cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, allspice, and clove, in different proportions depending on what you like in your pie. Mace is a rare but occasional visitor. Now that my annual pumpkin spice rant is out of the way, I will tell you that there is absolutely nothing wrong with preferring one type of pie over another. These little differences are what make the world go ‘round.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: How do you thicken beef stew? My other used to use cornstarch and a former employer used flour.
Answer: One way to thicken your stew is to dust the meat with seasoned flour before searing it. This essentially creates a roux which thickens the stew as it cooks. You can also simmer the stew uncovered during the last hour of cooking, allowing water to evaporate as it cooks. If it still isn't thick enough for your taste, remove most of the meat and vegetables with a slotted spoon, then whisk in buerre mani, small pieces of butter rolled in flour. You will need to cook it for several minutes to get rid of the raw flour taste, but it works well..

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Would angel food cake be a good or bad ingredient/cake for Tres Leche? What recipes are ideal for using angel food cakes?
Answer: You want a sturdier sponge for tres leches; something that can absorb all that liquid and still keep its shape. A basic white or yellow cake baked in a sheet pan does a good job. I've had a chocolate and cinnamon tres leches, which was unusual but very nice. Angel food cake is very light and airy. It's so delicate you need to cool it upside down so it holds its shape. It would collapse if you tried to soak it. Angel food cake made with citrus zest (orange, lemon, or lime) is very nice with just a dusting of powdered sugar. A vanilla version goes well with fresh berries and sweetened whipped cream.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What is the best baking stone for bread?
Answer: There is no one best baking stone. Anything that fits in the bottom of your oven, is food safe, and absorbs heat will do the job. You want a stone that is about 1/2″ (1.25 cm) thick. Some people use unglazed ceramic tiles with excellent results, but you need to be sure they are asbestos free and won't crack in the heat. The key to baking stones is to make sure they are fully preheated in order to provide a source of direct heat to the bottom of your bread. This takes about 45 minutes to an hour, unlike an oven, which will come up to temperature in about 15 minutes. Some people prefer baking steels, because they heat up faster, but the trade off is that they are heavier, so if you like to move the stone in and out of the oven, ceramic is preferable.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: If you make bread dough in a bread maker, do you need to punch it down before baking it?
Answer: If you're using the bread maker to mix and knead the ingredients, then letting it do a bulk fermentation in the machine, you will degas the dough as you take it out to shape. No further manipulation is needed, other than shaping the bread and letting it proof. If you are letting the machine do the full cycle from adding the ingredients to baking the bread, then you can just walk away and let it do its thing.

Answer: Like a frittata or an omelette, a quiche is just an eggy vehicle for flavors. You can add anything you like. There are some classic flavors, like ham or uncured bacon, gruyere cheese, caramel8zed onions and thevlike, but there's no reason why you can't use other ingredients, and take your quiche in new directions. An herb quiche is very nice, with parsley, thyme, cilantro, mint, or other greenery. You can add blamched veggies, asparagus, peas, or green beans in the spring, butternut squash in the fall, layers of parcooked yams or potatoes, anything you like, really. You do need to remember that goid cheese is an essential ingredient, and pick flavors that will harmonize with it, but that still leaves a world of possibilities to play with. Mushrooms, maybe. Question: Can dehydrated sourdough starter be used in the same way as dry yeast or does it need to be rehydrated?
Answer: Sourdough starter needs to be well fed and at full a activity before you use it to build a dough. So a dehydrated starter will need to be fed two or three times before being ready to use. Add a tablespoon or two of your dehydrated starter to about 30 grams each of flour and water, let it rest for at least eight hours at room temperature, feed it again, rest it for another eight to twelve hours, and add about 50 grams each of water and flour, give it five hours, and it should be ready to use. A. Active starter will have almost doubled in size, and will be full of bubbles. Remember to keep track of the amounts of water and flour used to build tge starter, so you can calculate that as part of your baker's percentage.

Question: Why do my pancakes turn out dense? How do I make them fluffy? Is there some trick not mentioned in the directions?
Answer: I'm not sure if you're making pancakes from a mix or from scratch. How you handle the batter makes a difference. If you beat it until it is smooth, your pancakes won't be as fluffy. Pancake batter should be mixed until it still has a few lumps in it. Then it needs to stand for about 15 minutes, to ensure that the flour is fully hydrated. In case you want to make pancakes from scratch, here's the recipe I use. If you want fluffier pancakes, whip the egg whites to stiff peaks and fold them in after you've combined the other ingredients. This recipe serves three or four people, depending on how hungry they are.. 250 grams flour (2 cups acooped & leveled) 2 large eggs 480 ml buttermilk (2 US cups) 1 1/2 tsp baking powder 1 tsp vanilla extract or 1/4 tsp almond extract 2 tbsp melted butter 2 tbsp granulated sugar Pinch salt (leave out if using salted butter) Combine the dry ingredients in one bowl, and the wet in another. Add the dry to the wet and stir until just combined. If you whipped the egg whites, fold in the egg whites. Let rest 10-15 minutes and preheat your pan or griddle. Use very little butter on the pan for even browning. This is a very flexible recipe. You can add spices like nutmeg, cinnamon, or allspice, you can add orange or lemon zest, you can use different kinds of flour. Sometimes I use a combination of rye and buckwheat, which is tasty. If you use whole grain flours, you may need a little more liquid.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What could happen if I accidentally fried (for example) chicken drumsticks with Apple juice instead of oil? By the gallon they look so alike! (Ok, not so much, but one could get confused😅)
Answer: Honestly? If you can't tell the difference between oil and apple juice you have no business deep frying anything. Frying is one of the more dangerous jobs in a kitchen. Take this test. Unscrew the cap of the jug. If you don't immediately smell apples, it probably isnt apple juice. Dip your finger in it (before adding it to a pot). If it feels thick and slippery, it's probably frying oil. Both of these tests assume that either someone has sold you bootleg juice or oil in an unmarked jug or you don't know how or can't be bothered to read labels.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: This last spring I bought a set of new cookware, that requires no oils/fats for cooking. Unfortunately not using these also removes a lot of the taste of fried foods such as eggs, fried potatoes. What are some spices that can replicate that taste?
Answer: Here's the thing. When chefs and cooks say fat equals flavor, they're telling you something about how flavor works. Many of the chemicals that make up the flavors in food, especially in spices, are fat soluble. This means that if you aren't cooking with fat, you're missing an opportunity to distribute that flavor through the food. If you're cutting back on cooking with butter and oil, you can't add back those flavors with spices, but you can make your food more interesting by thinking about how your dishes are balanced. A little bit of acid, in the form of vinegar ir citrus, can wake up flavors, as can the addition of fresh herbs at the very end of cooking or as a garnish. Spices should be stored whole, not as powders, snd toasting them before grinding them will bring out some of the more subtle flavors. One of the ways to wake up your taste buds is with a bit heat. Cayenne pepper, aleppo pepper, even a favorite hot sauce can work wonders. And you can always choose to use a little healthy oil. Olive oil, avocado oil, grapeseed oil, and a number of others fit on this list. Just because the cookware doesn't need oil is no reason you can't add it, in judicious quantities, to improve your food.

Question: Can grapefruit or lime juice be substituted for cream of tartar in a meringue? I don't have any lemons. It's for a banana pudding.
Answer: Any citrus juice will do the trick. All you need is a bit of acid to help stabilize the meringue. You can akip the acid entirely, and probably have no issue, the acid just makes it a little easier to get good stiff peaks.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: How many more ingredients are there in a homemade chocolate cake with chocolate icing, compared to a shop-bought?
Answer: It's far more likely to be the other way ‘round. A storebought cake will have added preservatives, and may include flavoring ingredients you don't have in your home kitchen. A home baked cake will likely include flour, eggs sugar, milk, baking powder, salt, butter or oil, milk, and whatever flavoring you use. Store bought cakes will have a much longer list of ingredients. Bakery cakes will be very similar to the ones you make at home, though good bakeries will likely use better quality ingredients unless you are buying premium butter and cocoa powder. Next time you buy a store bought cake, take a look at the list of ingredients, and decide for yourself.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What would whipping egg whites till they’re fluffy before folding into a cake batter achieve?
Answer: If you do it correctly, you are incorporating thousands of tiny air bubbles surrounded by protein, which will grow in the heat of the oven and help your cake rise better. If the recipe calls for cream of tartar, it's because a little bit of acid helps firm up the whipped egg whites. A few drops of lemon juice will do the same thing. Folding whipped egg whites into batter should be done in stages, not all at once. Stir one third of the whites into the batter to lighten it, then fold the rest of the whites in gently, retaining as much air as possible. This will keep your cake light and fluffy. It works for other things too, like pancakes and omelettes.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: How do you make homemade yeast for bread?
Answer: One answer is creating a sourdough culture, and feeding it regularly to maintain it. It's a bit like having a rather unresponsive pet, you need to take care of it. Fortunately, sourdough is easy. There are thousands of pages online telling you how to create a new culture. Some are fussy, and some are not. You can pick the level of precision you ferl comfortable with, but to be perfectly frank, all uou need to do is mix some whole grain flour with water, cover it to prevent things falling into it, and leave it alone for four or five days. That's what people did before they learned abput yeast and bacteria and how they work together. This method runs the risk of a few failures, but it's surprisingly workable. The less risky method is to measure equal weights of flour and water into a clean container, feed it every 24 hours with more flour and water for a week, then begin using or discarding part of tte mixture and feeding the rest. If you store your culture in the fridge you can feed it once a week. If you bake often, you can store it at room temperature but you need to feed it every 12 hours. As I said, there are thousands of online sites that tell you how to do this. Read a few, find one that suits your style, and get started. A second, less popular but equally easy method is to make a potato starter using commercial yeast. This involves boiling potatoes, mashing them with the water and some flour, and adding a packet of active dry yeast. Let it sit at room temperature and use a cup or two to make bread. It can be refreshed with more flour, mashed potatoes and the water from boiling, and you can store it in the fridge for a week or two. Some people prefer a potato starter because the added starch makes bread softer and retains liquid to retard staling. It lacks the tangy flavor of sourdough, but it's an interesting and historical method of managing home grown yeast. Again, you can find all kinds of recipes for potato starters and bread online.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Got a recipe with measurements in Y:2 cup and Y:3 cup. What does it mean and how to convert it to gram/oz?
Answer: Is the recipe scanned from hard copy? This is the kind of error that happens with poorly edited scans. Nobody that I am aware of uses Ys as a form of measurement in baking, nor can I find any examples online. I've been baking from all kinds of references, including translated Roman, Medieval and Renaissance cookbooks for more than fifty years, and I have never seen cups expressed as a value of Y. I could be wrong, and if so, I'd be delighted to see a link in the comments explaining this, but at the moment, it's a mystery. As to converting cups to grams, that can be problematic. Cups vary quite a bit internationally, so even if you interpret these as half cups or one third cups, or as two or three cups, the gram weights will be different, even for the same ingredients. Cups are standardized (sort of) by milliliters, but that is different from country to country. While we in the US use a cup equal to either 238 or 240 ml, our neighbors to the north in Canada use a 250 ml cup. And cups in Japan are smaller, I think 200 ml though I'm not entirely sure about that. I have a couple of suggestions. Track down the publisher and find out if you are using a badly edited scanned copy, then look for the original. Or, even easier, find a recipe with metric measurements. You'll save yourself a lot of agitation.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: How can I make a dome-shaped cake without a mould?
Answer: All you need is a stainless steel mixing bowl. You can bake in it, or you can line it with plastic wrsp, assemble a multilayered cake inside, then turn it out and decorate it wirh marzipan, frosting, or fondant. Easy peasy. Or, more complicated but no bowl needed, you can assemble the layers of your cake and carve it into any shape you want. There are even cakes that have domes of whipped cream or other filling covered with fondant or marzipan. You might also make a meringue dome on a flat cake, then bake it briefly. If you use a Swiss or Italian meringue, both of which are cooked in the process of making them, you can form your dome then brown it lightly with a kitchen torch. There are lots of possibilities.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Nine is measuring a milk to make pancake batter.the recipe calls for 3/4 glass of milk.he has 1/4 of a glass now.how much glass of milk is still needed?
Answer: Nine is in a lot of trouble. First, he or she has a silly name. Are they perhaps related to Seven of Nine, of Star Trek fame? Is Nine a Borg? I'm not saying it couldn't happen, but Nine is not a name, it's a number. Did Nine’s parents have eight older children, and simply run out of ideas for names when this little one came along? Secondly, is Nine following a recipe that calls for 3/4 glass of milk? That's just irresponsible recipe writing. Unusual, too. Most recipes measure liquids either in milliliters or in cups, not in glasses. A glass can be any size from a 2 ounce shotglass to a 12 ounce drinking glass, or anywhere in between. Even measuring in cups can be a problem, since measuring cups are different sizes in different countries. They range from 250 ml in Canada to somewhere between 240 ml - 238 ml in the States, to 200 ml in Japan. Nope. Nine is using a bad recipe. They need to toss it in the trash and find a pancake recipe written in metric, so they know how much milk they really need. Just a note: Quora is not a place to get answers to homework questions. And word problems should make sense in the real world, not just in the mind of someone who knows a little bit about math and nothing at all about cooking.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Edens wants to make fluffy pancake: how she will measure the 3 cups of flour needed?
Answer: Edens has a number of choices, depending on how she has been taught to cook, the equipment available in her kitchen, and how much ahe cares about getting her pancakes really fluffy. If she wants to do it granny style, she will grab a chipped, handle-less teacup from the shelf, measure her theee cups of flour into a sifter, and sift it into a bowl. If she's a devotee of Julia Child, she'll sift the flour into the cup, instead of the other way round. If she's mire modern, she may follow the Martha Stuart method, and scoop and level each cup of flour, or she might use a tablespoon to move the flour from the flour bin to the measuring cup. Of course, if she has a kitchen scale, she can simply put her bowl on the scale, set it to measure in grams, tare it so the weight of the bowl is subtracted from the total, and measure out 375 grams of flour. Whisking the flour, baking powder, salt, and sugar before adding wet ingredients will help fluff up the batter. If she really wants her pancakes fluffy, she will add a level teaspoon of baking powder for each 125 grams of flour along with a pinch of salt and two tablespoons of melted butter, and separate her eggs, adding the yolks with the buttermilk, then whisking the whites to stiff peaks before folding them into the batter, which should be the consistency of thick cream. If Edens (odd name, that) wants to take her pancakes to the next level, she can add slices of banana, fresh blueberries, chocolate chips, or any of a number of add-ins for more flavor and texture.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: In the US, is there a culture that when sharing the kitchen space with others, one leaves their dirty wares in the sink only to wash them days later?
Answer: Gaaah! No. Not in any house or apartment I've lived in, that's for sure. I'm pretty sure you can find slobs in just about every country on earth, not just in the US. But unless your roommates are also slobs and just don't care, leaving dirty dishes in the sink is going to cause complaints, fights, snd eventual eviction, by the roommates, if not by the landlord.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is it worth buying a 2mm lead pencil for sketching?
Answer: As with any art supplies, it's worth spending the money if it suits your drawing style. Pencils like this can be fitted with a variety of leads, not just graphite, so you can get a lot of different effects with the same tool. Most artists experiment with a number of materials and techniques, and it's always handy to have something like this in your arsenal. Mechanical pencils travel well, they don't make messes in your bag or pocket, and they are less prone to breakage than wooden pencils.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: When a recipe calls for scallions, what part do you use?
Answer: I use the while scallion, unless I want only the green part as a garnish. Scallions and sour cream are excellent toppings for savory bean soups, as an example. Peel off any shriveled outer leaves, remove the roots and dried ends, and slice or dice as needed. If I'm adding them to a sslad, I like to do the flower trick. Cut off an inch and a half of the white end, remove the root, and make several cuts lengthwise at right angles, leaving about half an inch uncut. Then drop the scallions in a bbowl of cold water to ‘bloom’.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is my bread a genuine whole wheat? It has two wheat ingredients, one is “whole wheat flour” and the second is ‘enriched unbleached wheat flour.’
Answer: Enriched, unbleached flour is flour that has had the germ and bran removed, and has additional vitamins and nutrients added to replace the nutrition lost in this process. It is not whole wheat flour. On the US, a lot of the whole wheat flour we buy is actually refined flour thst has had wheat bran and germ mixed back in, in order to maintain consistency in the product. To be fair, it is difficult to make a 100% whole grain bread without it being quite dense. Most whole wheat and whole grain bread on the market is a mixture of whole and refined flours, the actual percentage varying by type of bread and manufacturer. As long as the bread has a certsin percentage of whole wheat flour, it can be marketed as such. The required percentage will vary, depending on where you are. If it is labeled as 100% whole wheat, it will be a different type of bread. There are many delicious whole grain breads. But they aren't soft, sandwich style breads. They look more like this. My 100% rye sourdough You can find these breads at bakeries, especially those that specialize in eastern European baked goods. You are unlikely to find them in supermarkets, unless the market has a very good bakery attached. Your bread is whole wheat bread. It just isn't 100% whole wheat. It may be as little as 30% or as much as 60%, if it is an average supermarket loaf.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What are Halloween outfits you can make at home?
Answer: The types of costumes you can make is limited only by your imagination and your practical skills. You don't need to know how to sew. I have seen excellent costumes made with hot glue, glitter, and crepe paper, and mediocre ones hastily constructed with a sewing machine. Growing up, we made all our own costumes. These ranged from a three headed ghost with paper mache heads formed around balloons, to a complete Venusian invasion force with sashes, rank badges, and gold lame knickers (Get your minds out of the gutter, Anglosphere. Knickers are loose fitting knee length trousers.) One year, my brother was a space lettuce. He glued a bunch of crepe paper streamers to a headband, and looked like a colorful Cousin It from the Adams Family. One year in college, I found a lambskin coat at a thrift store, cut it up, and refashioned it into a Barbarian outfit, with a hat, vest, and fur topped boots. I spent the entire night making bad puns. The only one I remember, unfortunately, is a quip made while negotiating a flight of stairs after several drinks. “Barbarians hate stairs,” I exclaimed, “but we love steppes.” The key to creative costuming is inventive use of inexpensive materials, and in some cases, a little engineering know how. If you want to significantly change the profile of a costume (broad shoulders, angular shapes, tall silhouette) you need to construct an internal framework that is lightweight and comfortable. Frameworks are more comfy if constructed on a backpack frame, because if you put the weight on your shoulders, it quickly becomes uncomfortable. If all you want to do is be a classic ghost, vampire, or witch, you can assemble some costume pieces at a thrift store, add a bit of makeup, and be perfectly fine. Want to be a black cat? All you need is a leotard and tights, some whiskers, and a tail. Something more complicated? Draw it, then figure out how to put it together. Halloween is a chance to let your imagination off the hook, have fun, and show off a little. Decide what you want to be, then create something fun.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is rice gluten-free and wheat-free?
Answer: One of these things is not like the other. Rice is a grain. Wheat is a grain. They grow in different climates, have different nutritional properties, and are almost never processed in the same facilities. Rice does not contain gluten. Wheat contains proteins (glutenin and gliaden) that form gluten when combined with water. So do rye, barley, and other related grains. Rice does not contain gluten forming proteins. If you are buying products made with rice flour, all bets are off, because they may contain wheat flour or other grains, and they may be processed in plants that also process other grains. But if you are cooking whole grains, the chance of cross contamination is vanishingly low.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: If I took an uncut loaf of bread and very carefully sliced the entire loaf into a single helix and placed slices of meat and cheese between each of the folds, would it be a sandwich?
Answer: If I were marketing it, or the tool to make it, I would call it a “Spirewich.” But you can call it whatever you want. Spreading condiments on the bread might be a rather long term proposition. Just a minor quibble: There would only be a single, long fold.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is it easy to find real saffron for Milanese rice in the USA? How expensive is saffron in the USA?
Answer: It isn't difficult to find saffron in the US. HomePage | Penzeys currently lists it for about $21.00 per gram for Spanish coupe saffron, and slightly less for their Spanish Superior, which has the yellow end of the atyle still attached. You can buy less expensive powdered saffron, but it is likely to be cut with turmeric. Note: i have no connection with Penzey's, I just buy things from them on occasion.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Have you ever roasted your own pumpkin seeds?
Answer: I do it every time I carve a Jack O'Lantern, or make roast pumpkin. The trick is separating the seeds ftom the pulp, which is easiest if you soak everything in a bowl of water, and sort of of pop the seeds off the strands they are attached to. You can simply toss them with a bit of salt and toast them in the oven until golden brown and crisp, or you can add some spices. I like a combination of cayenne and smoked paprika, but you can use any flavors you enjoy.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Why aren't dried watermelon seeds sold like pumpkin seeds?
Answer: They are. We used to get them in Chinatown in New York City, with different flavors, some sweet, some salty. I'm sure you can find them in specialty markets, or at places like Trader Joe's, if you look.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Do salt, sugar, baking soda and cornstarch have something in common?
Answer: Well, they are all white, mostly. Sugar and salt come in a variety of colors. They are all finely granulated powders. Sugar and salt come in a variety of granule sizes and shapes. All of them are used in cooking and baking. All of them may be combined in a single recipe, along with other ingredients. All of them can be found in almost any well equipped kitchen. None of them can be substituted for another, as each has a specific job to do.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Can I use oil paint straight out of the tube as my first layer then add medium to it?
Answer: The general rule with oil paint is to layer fat over lean. This means using a medium with a higher percentage of turpentine in the underpainting, then adjusting it to a richer mix as you go. If you want to work with paint straight from the tube, you're better off continuing that in subsequent layers. You'll need to wait much longer for each layer to dry.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Can beef tallow and chicken schmaltz be used to replace lard in baking? Can it be used in the making of Cuban bread?
Answer: You can substitute either one for one with lard. They behave similarly in recipes. However, all three fats have distinctive flavors, so you will notice the difference.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What do Americans use for saffron in their paella dishes?
Answer: We use saffron. It's pricey, but readily available from most spice companies. I order mine from HomePage | Penzeys

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Would marinading a ribeye steak in Tzatziki (cucumber yogurt sauce) make it more tender?
Answer: I don't know that I would marinate a ribeye in anything. If I wanted added flavor, I'd probably use a dry rub instead. Ribeye is alteady nice and tender, as are most cuts cooked as steaks. I usually just salt steaks several hours in advance and serve them with herb butter. Not too fussy, and very tasty. Yogurt, like buttermilk, citrus juice, wine, or vinegar, is an excellent marinade for tougher cuts of meat, because it is acidic and breaks down the tough muscle tissues. The cucumber in tzatziki isn't going to contribute much flavor, but the garlic will.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What does it mean when someone's "two fries short of a happy meal"?
Answer: It means they are not operating on all cylinders, driving with one headlight, or one donut short of a dozen. In other words, functioning at less than optimal capacity, because they are either naturally stupid, drunk, or otherwise intellectually impaired. One beer short of a sixpack.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: I have a lot of jars of peanut butter. If I were to smear some of it on a tree or other surface during winter when food is scarce, would it attract animals to it?
Answer: Peanut butter will attract all kinds of animals. one of our annual crafts is to fill pinecones with peanut butter or lard and roll them in seeds. Hung in trees, they attract an assortment of birds and some very acrobatic squirrels. On the ground they attract raccoons, which isn't always the best idea, but they're fun to watch if your garbage cans are properly secured. For the record, they're on the ground because of the squirrels, not because we put them there.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Can carrots be fried like potatoes?
Answer: You can certainly fry carrots. You can fry anything. But carrots contain a lot of sugar, and less starch than potatoes, so you will get different results. If you want crisp carrot fries, I would try treating them like sweet potatoes. Soak them in cold water after cutting them into batons, parcook them in lower temperatire oil, cool them and pat them dry. Then toss them in a cornstarch slurry before frying them a second time. I haven't actually done this with carrots, but I do make sweet potato fries this wsy, and they're much crisper than those made without the cornstarch.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What is the correct texture for a bagel? I was disappointed today that a bagel from Woolworths (equivalent to M & S in the UK) was rather hard and chewy. I could barely manage the smoked salmon and cream cheese as a result.
Answer: A proper bagel should be chewy enough that it takes a bit of jaw muscle to bite into it. Good bagels are denser than most bread, but not hard. Bagels are fully proofed before being boiled, then baked. This means that though they rise after bring shaped, they don't get much oven spring, because boiling them sets the crust, as well as contributing to their shiny exterior. You shouldn't expect a bagel to be as soft as a loaf of bread. It should have some chew to it, just not too much.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: If you are learning to bake, is it better to start by using a boxed cake mix such as Jiffy or make it from scratch for your first few times baking?
Answer: I would recommend starting with simple scratch recipes. Pound cakes and quickbreads are very basic, and don't require much in the way of technique. Most cookies are fairly simple, and corn bread is dead easy. You can bake it in muffin cups or in a cast iron slillet. If you're going to use a mix, don't use Jiffy products. They're on the lower end of flavor snd quality. Look for mixes from Bob's Red Mill or King Arthur Flour. They have better variety, and better ingredients. KAF has some great scone mixes. The slightly sweet, crumbly, American style scones, not the British style.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is a breads’ final outcome greatly affected by how many times you prove the dough (what is the significant change in bread texture/taste if you prove the dough 0, 1, or 3 times)? Is there a maximum amount of times one can prove their dough?
Answer: Proofing the dough several times, or for a longer period at lower temperatures, develops the flavor and texture of the final product. Most recipes for home bakers call for a single bulk fermentation, then a proofing period after shaping tte loaves to allow them to rise. You can punch the dough down after it doubles during the bulk fermentation, and let it rise again hefore shaping it. You will get better results if you use active dry yeast, though I have done secondary fermentations using instant yeast (not quick rise or bread machine yeast) with no problem. Two bulk fermentations won't be a problem, but a third may leave your yeast with less food than it needs to proof the loaves. You need to experiment with a recipe and see what happens.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is White Castle good? They don’t have any where I live so I’ve never tried it.
Answer: My most significant memories of White Castle involve stopping there while my brother got a sack of a dozen sliders, and ate them on the way home from school. He always gave me one. Was it good? Ten year old Beth thought so. Soft, slightly sweet bun, savory meat patty, a single pickle slice in the center, and grilled onions. Maybe I just liked them because my big brother gave them to me. Adult Beth doesn't touch them. Haven't eaten one in over 45 years, since stoned college Beth shared a bag of them with a couple of friends. An overly sweet bun that's much too soft, tiny, greasy patty with holes in it, so it cooks fast and has less meat per burger; boring, unhealthy, and not worth the price, even as the cheapest slider in town. This is lowest common denominator food intended to be gobbled by the dozen, by the stoned and the drunk, to fill their bellies with carbs and grease and stave off hangovers. If that's what you're into, you might consider them good. White Castle is worth a single visit, if you happen to be driving by and just want to find out what the phenomenon is all about. But not if you're looking for a good slider, of which there are many these days, or good food in general. If you really want to know what they're like, they sell frozen versions. Yes, I know there are people who love these things, either out of nostalgia, or because they don't know any better, or just don't care. I'm not one of them. And even fans of the franchise would be hard put to assemble an argument for them being good food.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What does a 'chopped salad' consist of in the USA? Is it always the same recipe? Are there non-chopped salads?
Answer: In my family, a chopped salad is constructed in layers, in a clear glass bowl. The layers are made with diced vegetables, all cut to the same size. Ingredients include, but are not limited to: cucumbers, celery, bell peppers, tomatoes, cabbage, and carrots. It's put in the table with the veggies in neat colorful layers, then dressed and tossed before serving. The dressing can be anything you like. We usually use a light, lemony vinaigrette, but you can really use anything you like. 0ne iconoclastic cousin prefers French dressing. We eat his salad anyway, because otherwise we don't get his hazelnut amaretto cheesecake. Other people may have other definitions, but this is the recipe for chopped salad I learned from my Aunt Yetta, who was actually my first cousin, once removed. There are plenty of non-chopped salads in the US. You can create all kinds of tossed salads, usually made with some kind of leafy green like iceberg or romaine lettuce, and a few other vegetables. You can make hot and cold salads, tossing roasted vegetables in dressing, then adding them to chilled ingredients. You can make mayonnaise based salads like egg salad, tuna salad, potato salad, or Waldorf salad with apples, walnuts, celery, and grapes. Not associated with the Waldorf Astoria, though some think it originated there. You can even make Ambrosia, which is called a salad, but is actually a rather offputting combination of little marshmallows, canned fruit, and whipped topping, which some people claim is delicious. Some versions use sour cream instead of whipped topping. I don't see that as much of an improvement. There are wedge salads, made with a quartered head of lettuce topped with blue cheese dressing and crumbled bacon. There are the ubiquitous diner salads, consisting of limp iceberg, sad flavorless tomatoes, exactly two slices of cucumber and raw red onions. And there are numerous varieties of plated salads with all kinds of interesting ingredients arranged in interesting ways. Salad is what you make of it. This time of year, my favorite salad is made with roasted beets, toasted walnuts, and blue cheese crumbles, on a bed of red leaf lettuce. Toss the sliced beets in a mustard forward vinaigrette before adding them to the greens, toast the walnuts in a dry pan until they just begin to smell nutty, sprinkle the cheesy bits on top, and enjoy. Nothing in this salad is chopped.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Why do people mix strawberries and milk even though science says we are not supposed to mix citrus fruits with milk for making smoothies.I go to YouTube and I see that people are mixing all kinds of citrus fruits with milk why?
Answer: Strawberries aren't citrus fruits, so the question doesn't make sense. They do contain citric acid, but in much lower concentrations than citrus fruits such as oranges, lemons, limes, and grapefruit. Strawberries snd other acidic berries are often combined with dairy in yogurt and ice cream, so there's no reason not to add thrm to a smoothie. You can also make smoothies without dairy, using fruit juice instead.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: How do I buy a loaf of bread where all the slices are the heel?
Answer: I see a few options for this, none of which are very practical. If we weren't all shoppng under social distancing constraints, you might spend an afternoon at a local supermarket, asking people to give you the heels of any bread they bought. Since most people don't like the heels of bread, you might get some that way. An entire loaf worth? I have my doubts. The same might work at a bakery. You might even be able to get the counter people to separate the heels from the bread as they slice it, always assuming you got permission from ither customers. This approach also seems a bit dubious. A more practical approach would be to buy breads that are already designed to provide a high crust to crumb ratio, which is what you get when you eat the heels of bread. Kaiser rolls, sometimes known as hard rolls, would be a good solution. Slice one in half and you end up with two heel-like pieces. Baguettes are designed to provide a good crust to crumb ratio, as are any long narrow breads. Even better are the numerous flatbreads, which are essentially all heel. Lavash, pita, naan, chapati, and others are all excellent choices. Asking for a bag of bread heels at a supermarket or bakery is likely to confuse the staff, and may very well get you written off as a nutter. Asking for flatbread, of whatever sort, is perfectly acceptable, and will get you very similar results.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What could cause my attempt on this recipe to be so different (more watery) than the recipe photo? I used the precise quantities, temperatures, and times. The recipe is the braised chickpeas one.
Answer: It's always a good idea to bear in mind that food photography is a precise art. The kitchen may make several batches of a dish before getting one that looks good, and they may do a fair bit of manipulation. That doesn't mean the recipe isn't doable. It just means they've had several tries to get it right. Also, following a recipe precisely isn't as easy as many cookbooks make it seem. Your ingredients are not the same. They may have a different brand of canned tomatoes, a different type of chickpea, less watery vegetables. So you need to adjust things along the way, and learn what foid should look likes at varying stages of preparation. This isn't a problem with the recipe, and it's not a problem with how you prepared the dish. It's just a fact that cooking is less a matter of following precise instructions, and more a matter of learning how to msnipulate food to get the results you want. The recipe clearly says to bake until thick and rich. This is a bit ambiguous, and may not happen in exactly the time given for cooking. Chickpeas and other dried legumes will absorb more or less water, depending on how old they are, and how they were pre-soaked. That's why both sets of instrictions are included. In a braise like this, you want to give the liquid time to evaporate. Thus may involve removing the lid halfway through cooking, cooking for a longer time to make sure the liquid is absorbed by the legumes, or simply removing the cooked ingredients with a slotted spoon (if you're worried about over cooking them) and bringing the sauce to a boil on top of the stove. This will reduce it to the desired thickness, at which point you can add everything back to the pot, heat it up, and serve it forth.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: How can you use the whey leftover from making homemade yogurt?
Answer: Whey is useful stuff. It's tart and acidic, just like buttermilk. You can use it to add flavor to baked goods like muffins, biscuits (the American kind), bread, or pancakes. You can also use it to marinate chicken before dredging and frying it. And if you like tangy flavors and don't mind seeming a bit eccentric, you can chill it in the fridge and drink it.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Why do most croissant recipes state to not brush egg wash on the layered side of the croissants?
Answer: Egg wash will prevent the layers from separating if brushed on the cut edges of laminated pastry, like that used in croissants. You want the egg wash on top, to give your croissants that lovely, golden brown crust. But you also want the edges free to expand, so you need to be careful where you put the egg. The same is true when working wirh puff pastry. The recipe I use, which is from Baking With Julia, calls for brushing the egg wash on twice, once before the final rise, and once right before they go in the oven. They come out nice and brown, and shatteringly crisp around their lacy interior.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Does it have any effect if the croissant dough starts to proof during the rolling/shaping stage?
Answer: Croissant dough will already have undergone an overnight fermentation, before you begin the rolling and folding to create layers of butter and dough. The minute you add water and flour to yeast, it becomes active and begins its work of transforming the dough. This process continues, at one speed or another, until you pop the dough in the oven and bake it, which kills the yeast. Proofing is the stage where the dough has been shaped and is undergoing one final rise before baking. Fermentation happens at every stage, and if it isn't happening, there's something wrong with your dough. Becauae croissant dough is kept chilled between rolling and folding, it doesn't look as active as some orher doughs, but trust me. Even in the fridge, fermentation is going on. It's what makes croissants so tasty. Aside from all that butter, of course.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What do you normally do with the yolk or the white of an egg when you have a recipe that only requires the other?
Answer: I either: A. Add the unused portion to tthe next morning's scrambled eggs, or, B. Use it in another recipe, like fried rice, egg custard (savory or sweet) or a bread or cook8e recipe. Many recipes call for separating eggs, then using both whites and yolks in different parts of the recipe. If the recipe doesn't use the entire egg, you can always find a use for what’s left over.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Where and when did putting grated cheese on top of a casserole originate?
Answer: There are several dishes that include grated cheese in The Forme of Cury, a medieval recipe collection that exists in several editions. While none of them is exactly a casserole, the use of grated cheese in baked dishes certainly goes back quite some time in history. Casseroles, also known as hot dishes, became very popular in the US after WWII, since they made the most of inexpensive ingredients for feeding families. They were around before then, but the availability of less expensive, lighter weight cookware in the 50s certainly contributed to their proliferation.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What's a good web site to find recipes, and not a persons life story?
Answer: Any of the major food magazines will have recipes in a special, searchable section. It's usually at the top of their home page labelled, appropriately, “Recipes.” King Arthur Flour's Try it Once, Trust it Always is a great go to site for baking. Binging With Babish home of the Babish Culinary Universe (his name, not mine), is a fun site with eminently doable recipes for food from movies, TV, even video games. Check out the timbalo episode from Big Night, or his Lord of the Rings two-parter. Cooks.com isn't bad. They do a lot of recipe testing, so you know things from their site will work. Most blogs are about more than recipes. They're about people's personal take on food, culture, history, travel, family, and whatever else feels important to them. If you don't want to read what you consider extraneous information, you can always just skip to the recipes.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What can you do with leftover collard water? I removed all the collards, the ham hock, and have a lot of seasoned water that might be put to good use.
Answer: I had a friend in college who would strain the pot liquor, reheat it, and drink it from a mug, like savory tea. It's good served over cornbread, and you can use it to add flavor to a pot of rice, beans, or soup. You can also use it as a braising liquid. Pot liquor is good stuff.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: How do you work out how much dough to use in a pullman tin?
Answer: Generally speaking, on a second rise, or “proof,” the shaped dough will rise to not quite doubled in size, then get an extra burst of expansion in the heat of the oven. This is known as oven rise. You need to know your dough and judge how much it will expand as it proofs, remembering that the lidded pullman pan will prevent any oven rise. I usually want the shaped dough to fill slightly less than 2/3 of the pan, and rise during proofing almost to the top. That way, I know that the oven rise will help it fill the corners, producing a loaf with a nice square profile. You may need to experiment a bit with your recipe, until you know how it will behave. Remember to oil or butter the lid. I've forgotten once or twice, with regrettable results.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Will my bread autolyse if it’s too dry/dense?
Answer: Autolyse just means that the flour has a chance to absorb whatever water is in the recipe, so the answer to your question is yes. Sort of. If you aren't using enough water to properly hydrate the dough, it will still absorb liquid as it sits. The water will move from surrounding the individual grains of flour to plumping them a bit. But it won't do much good, as far as the texture of the final bread is concerned. The minimum hydration you want ought to be about 65%, expressed as a percentage of the total weight of flour, more if you want an airier crumb.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Should pre-cooked or uncooked rice be used in a casserole?
Answer: The rice you use depends on what else is in the casserole and how long it's going to be in the oven. I usually go for par cooked rice, unless I'm just heating a bunch of ingredients together. In that case, I would use fully cooked rice. I wouldn't use raw rice in a casserole because it may cook unevenly, due to the other ingredients, how much liquid you include, and other factors.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Why is the average American breakfast, coffee and roll (donuts)?
Answer: First, let's deal with the distinction between a roll and a donut. Rolls are made of bread, are not sweet unless they are sweet rolls (a separate, and delicious category*) and are definitely not donuts. You can get your bread roll with butter, cream cheese, ham, butter and ham, egg, egg and bacon, or plain. Donuts can be made with yeast risen dough or cake batter, are almost always fried, and can be iced with any number of things, filled with any number of things, or dusted with a short list of things, namely powdered sugar or sugar and cinnamon. Donuts are not rolls. Now as to this being the average American breakfast, it seems not to be the case. According to one survey I found, the average American only eats breakfast three times per week, and when they do, 68% of them say eggs are their preferred meal. So coffee and a roll (donuts are not rolls, rolls are made of bread) would seem not to be the typical choice. As to why coffee and some sort of hand held bready thing (roll, breakfast sandwich, donut, muffin, bagel, etc.) would be a common choice, that's easy to answer. It's fast, it's easy, you can eat it while commuting in your car, you don't need to sit down in a diner or cafe to order it. Convenience is king, if you're heading to work, dealing with rush hour, and dropping the kids off at school on the way. *About those sweet rolls. Too much for breakfast, in my opinion, but yummy as an afternoon snack. Brioche dough, rolled flat, brushed with melted butter, sprinkled with cinnamon and sugar, rolled into a spiral, sliced into individual rolls, then risen and baked in a pan with sticky caramel sauce in the bottom, which becomes the top of the roll when you turn them out. If you don't have one of these with good strong coffee every two months or so, you're definitely missing out on a treat. More often than that and it becomes excessive.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Should a bowl of sliced bananas be eaten with a spoon or fork?
Answer: Chopsticks. Definitely chopsticks. It will be good practice for eating those round, slippery mushrooms in sauce that are sometimes so problematic.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Can dried fruit be an alternative to regular snacks like popcorn and chips?
Answer: Popcorn is probably a healthier and more satisfying snack, provided you don't drown it it butter. Dried fruit has vitamins and minerals, along with dietary fiber, butit also has plenty of calories. You just need to he aware of the concentrated sugar and snack accordingly.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Which do you prefer for your breakfast sandwich, a croissant or a biscuit?
Answer: I actually prefer a bagel, or my homemade bread. I know what's in that, and it doesn't include preservatives, dough improvers derived from animal hair, or excess sugar. Croissants are delicious, but ahould be enjoyed for their buttery, flaky goodness, not made into sandwiches. The croissants used in most breakfast sandwiches, at least here in the states, are poor excuses for this most delicate and intricate of breads. The same is true of most biscuits, sad to say, if you're getting them at a fast food place. That may be bread of some sort, but it ain't no biscuit. Not a good one, at any rate. I had an egg and cheese sandwich for breakfast just the other day. Two slices of good bread toasted nice and brown, an egg folded around around melted gruyere cheese, a little mustard. Yum!

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Would you be brave enough to enter a bake off competition? What would be your winning category?
Answer: I've won a couple of cooking competitions, strictly at a local level. I've lost a few times, too, or at least not placed. It's fun to work on a recipe, see how you match up with the other cooks, and find new ideas based on the variety. My best pie was an heirloom tomato pie with a rosemary and parmesan crust and onion jam. Pretty yummy. I'm not really ambitious enough to go beyond the local farmers market, “What can you make wirh what's in season?” level. But it's entertaining to try.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Does putting a potato into a soup or sauce while cooking it reduce the saltiness?
Answer: If you add more ingredients, you increase the ratio of food to salt, so it will taste slightly less salty. But a potato, or any other starchy vegetable, won't actually pull salt out of your soup or sauce. Once you've added too much salt, the salt is there to stay. One solution for a soup might be to add plenty of a bland ingredient like rice, pasta, or barley. The real key is to taste as you go, and remember that sauces and soups reduce as they cook, concentrating flavors. If a pot of soup tastes salty enough at the very beginning, it will be too salty when it's done. Add a little bit of salt at each stage of cooking, taste your food often, and expect to finish seasoning it at the end, when it has reduced as much as necessary. Things like spices benefit from being cooked in the food, especially in fat which carries their flavor throughout the dish. Fresh herbs can be added during cooking, but also when the food is almost done, to retain their fresh flavor. And salt can wait until the end of cooking, when you taste your food and adjust the final seasoning.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is it acceptable to use the word "autumn" in American English?
Answer: Sure. Autumn is a good word and you'll find it in every English dictionary. Autumnal is nice too. Plenty of Americans use the word fall to describe the season, but lots of us use autumn as well. It's used to describe leaves, fashions, color palettes, and foods, among other things, like weather.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Why doesn't my soda bread rise?
Answer: Without a link to the recipe, it's hard to answer this. I can think of several possibilities. Irish soda bread is typically made with soft whole wheat flour, buttermilk, salt, and baking soda. Some recipes add baking powder, so you get some additional lift from the heat of the oven. Handling the dough too much will develop gluten, which makes the dough stiffer and may affect how much it rises. You want to mix it just enough to form a coherent dough, shape it, cut it almost all the way down, and put it in the oven as quickly as possible. Not preheating your oven long enough will mean thst it isn't hot enough to get a good rise. Make sure the oven is up to temperature before you begin mixing the dough. Using a baking stone for good bottom heat will help your bread rise, but it needs at least 45 minutes to soak up the heat of the oven. A baking steel heats up faster. Do not substitute regular milk for buttermilk, unless you also add a tablespoon of vinegar for each cup of milk in the recipe. Baking soda needs acid to work properly. The recipe I use, from James Beard’s Beard On Bread uses one teaspoon of baking soda plus 3/4 teaspoon of baking powder for 500 grams (4 US cups) of flour. Try that ratio and see if it helps.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Am I supposed to wash the cabbage before making sauerkraut to get rid of worms and parasites?
Answer: It's totally up to you, and probably depends on where you get your cabbage. Canbage isn't known for harboring parasites, but it can be dirty on the outside. Rinse it off and slice it in half. If it looks dirty on the inside, you can quarter it, then soak the quarters in a bowl of water. That won't do it any harm. I usually remove a few outer leaves, rinse the whole head in cold water, then proceed to quarter and shred it. I've never found any worms in my sauerkraut. Remember, you'll be fermenting the cabbage in brine, which is going to destroy most bacteria other than the lactobacillus that are doing the actual work of fermenting your sauerkraut. As long as you use the proper weight of salt ( 3% of the weight of the cabbage) you shouldn't have any problems.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What's the best way to machine wash a vintage chenille bedspread?
Answer: Washing it in a machine would depend on its age and condition. Vintage can include a broad range. If the spread is in good condition, with no thin spots, holes, or frayed edges, I would wash it on a gentle cycle in cold water. If it isn't in good condition, you can wash it the way my mom treated her handmade yoyo coverlet, the one she finished after inheriting a partial one from her mother. Fill your bathtub partway with warm soapy water. Put the spread in rhat, and let it soak for an hour without agitating it, then drain, rinse, and repeat until the water runs clear. Roll the spread up, squeeze as much water out as you can, then hang it up to dry. This takes longer, but it won't damage the spread.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Answer: How about a leek and onion tart? It's delicious hot or at room temperature, and makes a nice appetizer or side. Start by caramelizing a big batch of onions and leeks, sliced about 1/4″ thick. Remember that they will shrink considerably as they cook, and judge the amount accordingly. Cook them with a large pinch of salt on medium low heat until they turn golden brown and very tender. You can add some minced rosemary, thyme, or sage, according to your personal preference. When they are done, taste and adjust the seasoning, adding salt and fresh ground black pepper to taste. Make a tart case by rolling out a sheet of store bought puff pastry between 1/4″ -1/8″. Use a sharp knife or a pastry wheel to cut it into a 10″ x 5″ rectangle, and cut half inch wide strips to form the edges. Use an egg wash to make sure the edges stick to the bottom, fill the tart case with the onions and leeks, and brush the top of the pastry with the egg wash. Be careful not to drip it on the sides, because that will keep the pastry from puffing nicely. Bake the tart in a preheated, 400°F oven for about 20 minutes, until the pastry is golden brown and crisp. It's yummy served as is, or you can top it with arugala tossed in a light vinaigrette or a poached egg.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What is the American English for pocket money?
Answer: We call it an allowance, a sum of money kids recieve on a weekly or biweekly basis. I'm not sure how common the practice is these days, because some kids seem to just ask for cash when they need it or order stuff online with their parents’ credit or debit card. We're moving closer and closer to a cashless society, so keeping real money in your pocket is beconing less common. I do know a dad I worked with who kept bitching about downloading credit into his kid's phone for gaming, but he didn't consider that part of his allowance.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Why did Yankee Doodle call it macaroni when he stuck a feather in his cap?
Answer: Macaroni was a slang term for the fashionable young men of the 1760s. Returning to Britain after the then standard grand tour of Europe, they wore slimly tailored silks, satins and lace, and full, exaggerated wigs. They also imported foreign foods, including the pasta that gave them the name. A doodle was a popular term for a simpleton or fool. The song is mocking the colonials who dressed in linen and wool, and couldn't afford fancy duds and lace trimmed cravats. The song was reclaimed during the revolutionary war, and used as a patriotic anthem. “Fath'r and I went down to camp, along with Captain Gooding,/And there we saw the men and boys as thick as hasty pudding.” The hasty pudding refers to a atrictly colonial food made with cornmeal and maple syrup, both new world foods, which is an interesting touch. It's worth noting that in later years, macaronis themselves came in for a good deal of mockery, including cartoons of their extreme fashions, and humorous articles expressing doubts about their masculinity, at a time when homosexuality was a crime punishable by death or imprisonment.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Unfortunately, Jana is making cookies using a recipe that calls for ¾ cups of sugar. If she doubles the recipe, how much sugar should she use?
Answer: I'm perplexed. Why is it unfortunate that Jana is making cookies? Is the questioner hoping for a sandwich instead, or a bowl of soup? I would be overjoyed if Jana came to my house and baked me some cookies. When she did, I would give her my kitchen scale, inform her that one US cup of granulated sugar weighs 200 grams, and let her do her own math.
