Question: Should you put a glass of water in the oven when making bread?
Answer: A glass? No. I would be afraid it would break. You want a metal pan that sits on the bottom of the oven. You let it preheat in the oven, then about 30 seconds before you put the bread in to bake, you toss a handful of ice cubes in the pan. Close the oven door, count to thirty, then put the bread in. Even better is using a Dutch oven or a ceramic cloche to bake your bread. You don't need to mess around creating steam. Both seal in the moisture that's already in the dough, promoting good oven rise and a nice sturdy crust. You can even use an oven proof bowl, turned upside down over the bread on a steel or stone. Just make sure that whatever you use is preheated for at least 45 minutes.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Why do my biscuits develop a rock hard consistency so quickly? These are ones made from store bought mix.
Answer: I don't know how quickly your biscuits harden, but they are meant to be baked and eaten right away. Biscuits don't store well at all. James Beard wrote in Delights and Prejudices that his mother made them three times a day, instead of holding over breakfast biscuits for lunch or lunch hiscuits for dinner. If you like biscuits, google his cream biscuit recipe. They're delicious. Hot out of the oven, biscuits are marvelous. Let them sit for a few hours, and even rewarmed, they aren't quite as good. By day two, they're only good for bread and butter pudding. If you need to make a big batch of dough, and can't finish all the biscuits, your best bet is to make the aforementioned bread pudding, or use them as stuffing, or add them to ground meat for meatballs, meatloaf, or stuffed peppers.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Do biscuit s’mores exist?
Answer: Are we talking about British biscuits, like a Rich Tea or a Digestive? I can see that working. All you need is a crunchy, fairly neutral base for the melted chocolate and toasted marshmallows. Even Hob Nobs might work, though that would be pushing it. I wouldn't do it with a Ginger Nut, which is my favorite British biscuit, because the flavor would be all wrong. As for American biscuits, they're too bready to make a s'more, but I see no reason why you couldn't sandwich melted chocolate and a toasted marshmallow inside one, if it was hot from the oven. Might be very tasty and indulgent, with all that butter and buttermilk. But it wouldn't be a s'more.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Do you use spreadable butter or regular butter for a grilled cheese sandwich?
Answer: Regular butter is spreadable at room temperature. Just take the butter out of the fridge and let it sit on the counter in a butter dish. It will be good for at least a week, longer if it's salted. No need for spreads that are butter flavored, or softened by adding things other than butter to the product. I made a grilled cheese sandwich for lunch today. Stone ground mustard, cheddar cheese, beefsteak tomatoes, on home baked anadamma bread. Cooked with real butter. It was yummy. Why would I use anything else?

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What can I do when my cakes shrink and falls after baking?
Answer: Once a cake has fallen, there's not much you can do to fix it, but you can accept that you have a dense delicious cake and serve it forth without apology or explanation. After all, nobody knows how it was supposed to turn out. Fill the hollow center with fresh berries, and dust it with powdered sugar, or cover the cake with whipped cream, flavored with a bit of sugar and a tablespoon of brandy or cognac. Thoroughly drain a package of frozen cherries, add them to the top of the cake, and decorate them with chocolate curls. I guarantee that no one will think the cake is a flop. Now, about preventing future collapses. There are several reasons why cakes sink after being taken out of the oven. It may not be fully baked. Make sure a tester inserted into the center of the cake comes out clean, with just a few crumbs and no wet batter on it. Check that the edges of the cake have begun to pull away from the pan, and touch the center gently. It should feel firm and springy. The cake may have too much leavening in it. If you add more baking soda or baking powder, in the hope that it will make a cake lighter, it rises too high, then can't support its own weight. The edges hold their shape and the center sinks. Check your recipe to make sure you are measuring all the ingredients correctly, and if the cake collapses regularly, get another recipe. The cake may need to cool a bit before being removed from the pan. This prevents oven shock, the change of temperature from oven to countertop, since the pan retains heat. Let it cool in the pan for about ten minutes, then turn it out into a cooling rack. Some cakes benefit from being left in the cooling oven, with the door propped open by a wooden spoon, but that will depend on your recipe. Always remember that home ovens are not consistent in temperature, and knowing when your cake is done is a matter of testing, not precise timing. It's a good idea to check a few minutes before you think it's done, then give it more time if necessary.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is it possible to make a brioche bread without a stand mixer?
Answer: Brioche has been around since at least 1440. That's when it is first mentioned in writing, which means it probably existed for a minimum of several decades before the recipe was written down. The original recipe may have included brie as well as butter, which sounds amazing. Unless they were in an alternate timeline, I can pretty much guarantee that bakers in the 15th century had no stand mixers. What they did have were strong arms from kneading large masses of dough on a daily basis, apprentices with strong arms from hauling wood for the ovens, mixing dough, sweeping the floor of the bakery, and all the other menial chores that needed to be done. They would also be equipped with plenty of mixing bowls and sturdy wooden spoons and paddles, plus a baker's most important tools, which they keep on the ends of their arms. (Hint: they have fingeys) Yes, you can make brioche without a stand mixer. It's not easy, since incorporating all that butter in a soft sticky dough takes a fair amount of work. I have broken a very sturdy wooden spoon doing this. Nowadays, if I don't have a stand mixer, I use a bowl scraper. It does a decent job. It takes quite a while. But it is doable. Stand mixers are much easier. If you want to try making brioche by hand, you can start with what's known as poor man's brioche, made with about one-third the amount of butter. The dough is easier to handle, though it isn't as rich as the full on butter bomb of a richer brioche. Once you've tried that, you'll know if you have the patience (and the guns) for a full butter brioche.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Should I make my dinner guests wait to eat if I am still waiting on one more guest?
Answer: This is one of those situations where you just have to play it by ear. If it's a formal dinner party, and the food is time sensitive, you don't want to delay eating. If the special guest is delayed, you probably want to wait. If it's just a casual get-together, and the food won't be ruined if it is kept warm for half an hour, then serve some extra nibbles, open a bottle of wine, and tell everyone dinner will be a little late. If someone is habitually late (I have a couple of these friends) then go ahead and have dinner. They can eat when they get there.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What are some inventions that are even better than the wheel and sliced bread?
Answer: Top of my list is indoor plumbing, especially the flush toilet. Also, no-iron cotton sheets, flannel pajamas on cold winter mornings, and a reliable system to get good quality coffee into stores on a regular basis. I can slice my own bread very well, thank you.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Would a 11 7/8"Dia.× 2 3/ 8" depth pan work for a turned out pineapple upsidedown cake?
Answer: Most pineapple upside down cake recipes call for an 8″ or 9″ pan. So unless you double the recipe, you will end up with a very thin cake. But the cake part of a classic upside down cake is just a standard yellow sponge. Just look for a recipe for yellow cake that makes two 9″ layers, use about 2/3 - 3/4 of it to make your cake, and use the rest for a few cupcakes on the side. Pretty much any birthday cake recipe will give you enough batter to do that. It's a good idea to butter the bottom of the pan, add a circle of parchment paper in the bottom, then butter the parchment. Makes unmolding the sticky, caramelized cake much easier.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is it true that most American households don't have accurate kitchen scales, and that is why American recipes use volumes rather than weights?
Answer: To begin with, I have to say that the kitchen scales available in the US are as accurate as any other kitchen scales. Maybe I wouldn't want to use one for a science experiment, but for everyday accuracy, they measure up just fine. They're also inexpensive, so anyone who wants a scale can get one. Many people just don't see a need. In my opinion, most Americans don't use scales in the kitchen unless they are enthusiastic bakers. Those of us who bake regularly know that weight is more accurate than volume, and it's important when measuring things like flour, where the amount of an ingredient can vary considerably if using volume measurements. On the other hand, most of us who learned to bake using volume know this, and know how to compensate for it, so the scales aren't that big a deal. I have plenty of volume recipes that work reliably every time, because I always measure ingredients the same way, and I know what a dough or batter is supposed to look and feel like. We (Americans) get a lot of these metaphorical raised eyebrows because we insist on using cups, tablespoons, and pinches, as if we only do it because we don't know what we're doing. But volume measures have been a thing since Fanny Merritt Farmer first published her Boston Cooking School Cookbook in 1896. It's worked well enough for over a century, for thousands, nay millions, of home cooks. The Fanny Farmer Cookbook has been in continuous publication since that first edition. It works. Yes, I own a kitchen scale. I use it for baking bread, because ratios and percentages are important. I don't use it for anything else, unless I'm using a recipe that has measurements in grams and milliliters. If you know what you're doing, switching between the two is effortless. To scale, or not to scale? Does anybody really care, as long as the food is tasty? Not me.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Do you consider sweet corn a proper pizza topping?
Answer: I wouldn't do it. It just seems odd. Since pizza is a traditionsl Italian dish, and corn is a new world food, it seems out of place. On the other hand, one of the best pizzas I had in Italy was made with thinly sliced potatoes, rosemary, and garlic. It was excellent. So I wouldn't put sweet corn on pizza, but if you like it, go ahead. It's your pizza, after all.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Can I do a yogurt-based marinade in a stainless steel container?
Answer: Stainless steel is nonreactive, so it's fine for acidic marinades using things like yogurt, citrus juices, wine, or vinegar. Glass bowls also work. Just stay away from aluminum.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is it true that onions absorb viruses and prevent illness?
Answer: Once upon a time, someone loaded a barge with raw onions and floated it down the Thames, in an attempt to draw off the miasmas that caused the plague. Fortunately, we know better now. Onions do not absorb viruses. But they are very tasty.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: While hurriedly giving a tour before it's too dark to see, is it rude to get upset at your guest asking 12 questions about wood size & accessibility while they drive quickly past landmarks key to the guest's favorite hobby usage on your property?
Answer: It's not exactly clear what's going on here, but if it is a paying guest, it's certainly not best practice to show how annoyed you are. In the first place, why is the tour taking place so late? As a guest, I would expect better planning from my host, or an explanation along the lines of, “It's too late to do a proper tour right now. Why don't we do a quick cruise around the property and I'll answer all your questions once you get settled in.” Clearly, the guest's interests are not exactly what you expected. That shouldn't be a problem. Maybe you should provide a good map, and let them explore the landmarks by themselves. In any case, if you are in the hospitality industry, learning to deal with annoying people is part of the business. If you're good at it, you can send them away satisfied without ever letting them know they got under your skin. If I'm mistaken, and the guest is a friend, it ought to be easy to let them know it's getting too dark, and you can continue your tour in the morning.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What’s the best way to keep homemade cake from drying out, besides making sure it’s covered?
Answer: One of the easiest ways to keep a cake from being dry is to brush it with simple syrup. You can flavor the syrup with vanilla beans, with rum, brandy or the liqueur of your choice, with citrus juice and zest. Just make sure the flavors in the syrup complement the flavor of the cake. You can also use jam or jelly, thinned with a little water. Apricot or raspberry are traditional, but I make a dark chocolate cake that I brush wirh bitter orange marmalade thinned with a little brandy that's a big favorite, though it isn't really child-friendly. The kids usually end up with slightly sweeter chocolate cupcakes. If you plan to frost the cake, brush it with syrup while it's still slightly warm, then chill the layers before frosting.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What are a few ways to make a traditional peanut butter and jelly sandwich more imaginative?
Answer: Start by upgrading your ingredients. Home baked bread, jam or preserves made with freah fruit, different kinds of nut butters. Peanut butter is very easy to make at home, and you can keep it plain, using only roasted peanuts and salt, or you can add spices like cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, even savory spices like cayenne pepper. Try something other than white sandwich bread. A hearty whole grain sourdough, a cinnamon raisin loaf, or walnut soda bread are all good choices. You might want to lose the jelly entirely, and go the savory route. Peanut butter and bacon perhaps, without the bananas.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: How do you make a skirt without a pattern?
Answer: The simplest skirt in the world is a sarong, a straight piece of fabric long enough to wrap around your waist at least two times. You can find instructions for wrapping them online. If isn't purpose made, you will need to hem the edges. A straight tube wide enough to fit around your hips with either an elastic or drawstring waist is almost as simple. No pattern needed, just some basic measurements. If you want something fancier, look for circle skirt calculators. They will show how to cut a circle skirt, calculating from your waist measurement. All you need is a piece of paper, a pencil, and a ruler. Circle skirts are fairly basic. If you have a comfortable skirt you like to wear, you can use it as a pattern, with a few adjustments. You need to remember to add seam allowances, figure out a waistband, and if needed, insert pockets and closures. If you aren't confident about that, you really need to buy a pattern with step by step instructions.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What is the difference between bechamel and hollandaise sauce?
Answer: Bechamel starts with a light roux, and is made with milk. It gets its flavor from onion, bay leaf, snd clove, along with a hint of nutmeg and white pepper. Hollandaise is a liaison of egg yolks and butter, flavored with lemon juice, white pepper and a dash of cayenne, according to Julia Child. They are two very different sauces, and both are the starting point for dozens, if not hundreds of variations. Bechamel is also a lot easier to master.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: When someone gives you a gift of preserves or some other homemade "canned" food, what is the correct etiquette? Are you expected to return the glass ball jar and lid?
Answer: When I give someone a jar of jam or other preserves, I consider the jar as part of the gift. I don't expect it back But since my niece and sister in law are both also food gifters, I do get canning jars in return. Are they the same jars? Usually not. But as long as I can replace the lids, they're still useful.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is it true that trinkles can last forever? What makes it so highly preserved?
Answer: Forever is a very long time. No Twinkies can't last forever. But they are full of preservatives that keep them moist and fresh for a long time, sealed in their plastic packaging. The forever nonsense is just hyperbole.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What's a tasty ingredient to add to the milk and eggs for French toast?
Answer: I'm a fan of nutmeg and a teeny, tiny hint of almond extract for sweet French toast. But I slso like to make a savory version with fresh thyme and cayenne or smoked paprika. After its fried, I top it with grated gruyere and put it under the broiler for a minute, just until the cheese turns a nice golden brown. It's good with a broiled tomato on the side.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is pita bread considered real bread?
Answer: Define real. it sounds like your definition is different than mine. Pita is made with flour, water, salt, and yeast, just like most other breads. The difference is in the shaping.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What grocery stores sell halvah?
Answer: Many of them have those Joyva halvah bars in the candy aisle, but it isn't very good halvah. You just need to check individual stores to see if they stock it. If you have a Middle Eastern specialty store in your area, that's probably the best place to look. If not, you can make halvah easily, if you have a candy thermometer. This is almost Andy Baragani's recipe, from Bon Appetit. I'm doing it from memory, because of the appalling BA fiasco. 1 1/2 cup sesame tahini 1/4 cup black sesame seeds 1 cup sugar plus 1/4 cup water 1/4 tsp salt 1/2 cup sugar 1/2 cup water Dried rose petals for decoration Line a loaf pan with parchment psper before you start. Combine the salt, tahini, and sessme seeds in a bowl. Reserve a tablespoon of the seeds for decoration. Bring the sugar and water to a boil over medium heat. Brush down the sides of the pan with water to eliminate sugar crystals and bring the syrup to 245°F. Stream the syrup into the tahini, stir until it pulls away ftom the sides of the bowl, and press into a parchment lined loaf pan. Sprinkle with the reserved sesame seeds, a little sea salt, and the rose petals to serve. This is also nice with grated lemon zest instead of the sesame seeds. You can substitute your choice of chopped nuts for the sesame seeds.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: A and B are friends. A asked B to give a box of chocolate to C, but B delivered the box of chocolates to D. What was the obligation of D, and why?
Answer: D has no obligation, other than to enjoy their box of chocolate. But B either owes the price of the chocolates to A, or another box purchased with their own money to C. Also, B should apologize to C, for the angry text A sends when they don't get a thank you from C for the gift. How did D get involved in this mess anyway? Is B trying to hook up with D, thinking A's chocolates will do the trick? Can B not afford their own chocolates? If A and B are friends, why is B giving the chocolates to the wrong person? Does B have something aganst C? Is B simply so poorly educated that they couldn't read the address on the box? Why isn't A giving the chocolates to C themselves instead of trusting this delicate errand to the unreliable B? Have none of these Letterites heard of Amazon or Instacart? A could have had the chocolates delivered directly to C's door, without the interference from that nogoodnik B, who is clearly set on alienating A from C. Or C from A. Whatever. Amazon would even include a gift card, so C knew who their chocolatey benefactor was. I hope A and C can reconcile after the tiff caused by B"s mismanagement of this seemingly unmanageable task. It would be tragic for them to be torn apart at this delicate, third party chocolate delivery stage in their relationship. I hope A doesn't get too angry with D, who only ate a box of chocolates they thought was for them. Does A even know D? It's a mystery. With any luck, B has the grace to apologize to all concerned, and the wherewithal to buy a really big box of good quality chocolate to share with A, C, and D. Outside, and at an appropriate safe distance.

Question: What is the science behind no-knead bread?
Answer: There are already a couple of good answers addressing the effect of a long fermentation on the alignment of gluten molecules, which makes the dough easier to work with. They aren't wrong, but they miss some of the subtleties. There's more going on in the dough than relaxation of the gluten network. The action of tiny bubbles of CO2 rising through the dough actually helps strengthen the gluten, as does the action of enzymes released by the yeast. This is why no knead dough works; it gets stronger and more elastic as it ferments. Something else is happening at the same time. Have you ever tasted raw flour? It doesn't have much flavor, because the molecules it is made of are too large to interact well with our taste buds and the aroma sensors in our noses. For that, you need smaller, simpler molecules. Yeast does that, digesting the larger, more complex molecules onto simpler ones we can taste. It's why no knead bread can develop such wonderful flavors without being enriched by eggs, dairy, sugar, or other ingredients. Lastly, there's the baking process using a preheated dutch oven. This is basically an oven in an oven, creating an intense, even heat while trapping steam. This keeps the dough moist to encourage oven spring, imitating the steam injection ovens used by professional bakers. The longer the crust stays flexible, the more the air trapped inside the dough can help it rise.

Question: What is a gluten-free bread with actual nutritional value?
Answer: Let's begin with a clarification. Everything you eat, unless it's a non-food item, has some nutritional value. Even a spoonful of sugar has nutritional value. It's all carbs, snd carbohydrates are one of the macronutrients your body needs to survive, the other two being lipids (fat) and protein. Admittedly, eating pure carbohydrates with no other nutrition isn't efficient and can be very unhealthy if you do it too often, bit it's still a nutrient. What you want is a gluten free bread that also contains vitamins, minerals, dietary fiber, snd other good things in addition to carbohydrstes. Corn tortillas, made with nixtamalized corn, would fit the bill. So would any bread made with an enriched gluten free flour blend. Coconut flour is frequently used as a substitute for wheat flour, and while you csnt make good yeast raided bread with it, you can make decent quick breads, if you remember to boost the liquid content to allow for greater absorbency. The most popular gf bread at the moment seems to be almond flour keto bread, made with whipped egg whites. Nreads with whole grains, nuts, and seeds are very nutritious, and there are a number of them on the market. You just need to decide what you like, and what's a good match with the rest of your diet.

Question: How clean is clean when it comes to checking if a cake is baked?
Answer: Ah… That mysterious statement, “A tester comes out clean.” What exactly does clean mean? Well, it depends on the cake. With some cakes, like a typical butter or oil based sponge, you should expect the tester to be dry, without any wet batter clinging to it. There may be a couple of crumbs. Other signs to look for are a top that springs back when pressed lightly, and edges that have pulled away from the edge of the pan Wetter cakes may leave your tester damp, but still without batter on it. Sticky cakes like honey cake may fail the clean tester test, as will things like brownies and flourless cakes. With those, you need to rely on set edges and the genersl appearance of the cake.

Question: Why cake flour is a good substitute for bread flour in bread making? Why?
Answer: Cake flour is absolutely not a substitute for bread flour when making bread. Flours are classified according to the amount of protein they contain, which translates to gluten content. Most bread (strong) flours have at least 11.5% protein, and sometimes as much as 14%. All purpose (plain) flour can range from about 10.5% to 12%. Cake and pastry flour will always be below 10%, and often lower. These percentages will vary from country to country, and from company to company. Protein (gluten) content determines how sturdy your bread dough will be, and how well it will rise. It makes a difference in the chew of the crumb, and in the ability of the dough to trap air. If you want to make soda bread or quickbreads raised with chemical leaveners, you can use cake flour for those, since they don't depend on a well developed gluten network for their rise, and are more cakelike in texture.

Question: How do you draw sharp lines with charcoal?
Answer: If you use charcoal pencils instead of vine charcoal, they come in several hardnesses. You can sharpen the harder ones to pretty good points. But you'll never get as sharp a line with charcoal as you would with some other media, like ink pens or hard pencils. It just isn't the nature of the medium. Charcoal also works best on paper that has some tooth to the surface. You get crisper lines on paper with a polished surface, but charcoal isn't the best thing for drawing on slick papers.

Question: Does a deli count as a fast food restaurant?
Answer: It depends. Are you defining food as anything that can be produced quickly enough to satisfy customers during a lunch rush? In that case, deli sandwiches, burritos, falafel, and a bunch of other street food turned restaurant fare qualifies. If you limit the definition to chain restaurants, then maybe not. Delis usually have more than one option for dining. Sure, you can grab a sandwich and a bag of chips at the counter, but you can also sit down and enjoy table service. Many of them operate as family restaurants where you can eat your meal, then sit and chew the fat while you enjoy each other's company. That's not a typical fast food experience. And much of the food at a deli isn't fast in terms of cooking. Katz's Delicatessen, for instance, makes their own pastrami and corned beef, a days long process of brinng, seasoning, smoking (in the case of pastrami). In other words, slow food, not fast food.

Question: When kneading my bread. It always comes out sticky and 1/2 the dough is on my hands. What am I doing wrong?
Answer: It sounds like you're working with a high hydration dough, and they can be quite sticky in the initial stages of kneading. You're not doing anything wrong, you're just not being patient enough. You might want to look at some videos of the French slap and fold kneading technique. You'll see that in the beginning, the dough is very sticky, and the baker's hands are covered. As you work the dough, it becomes tacky instead of sticky, and less of the dough sticks to your hands. A bench scraper to get the dough off the counter at frequent intervals is very useful in this process. But with wet doughs, you do need to be comfortable with the dough on your hands. It just does that. Another option is the stretch and fold technique, used for doughs that will have a long fermentation. With this technique, you use an autolyze of 30 munites to let the flour and yeast absorb the water, then you add the salt, let it rest for 30 minutes, then do three or four stretch and folds at 30 minute intervals. You dip your hands in water before stretching the dough, so it doesn't stick. Again, there are plenty of videos online, so you can see how it works. I recommend looking at Foodgeek on YouTube. He does a lot of experimenting with timing, kneading techniques, and high hydration sourdoughs. Foodgeek

Question: What pepper has a high capsaicin but low on the Scoville scale? I want the health benefit of capsaicin without destroying the taste of my food. Perhaps there is a middle ground.
Answer: The Scoville Scale is a measure of the capsaicin levels of the peppers, so peppers that are low on the scale will be liwer in capsaicin. If you're looking for peppers that are enjoyable to eat while having manageable heat kevels, that's a matter of personal taste and local availability. You'll need to experiment with what you find at your local market. All peppers, even bell peppers, have some capsaicin. You can buy a number of different mild peppers, like poblanos or ancho chiles, or you can get spicier, but still tasty Fresno chilis or habaneros. They all have slightly different flavors and heat levels. If you just want capsaicin for its supposed medical benefits, there is no recommended dosage, but you can buy capsules. If you do, I suggest doing your research, as taking concentrated capsaicin can have some unpleasant side effects.

Question: What is bone broth, exactly, how is it different from ordinary chicken or beef broth (which includes bones in the cooking), and why did I never hear of it until the last couple of years?
Answer: Honestly? I have no idea. Epicurious has a recipe for bone broth that looks just like standard beef stock, with roasted bones and aromatic vegetables, a few herbs, and a long cooking time to extract maximum flavor from things like oxtail, shortribs, or knuckle bones. Other sites have recipes using the chicken bones from your roast chicken. Some recipes include apple cider vinegar, some don't. Some claim that adding vinegar pulls more nutrients out of the bones. It doesn't. It's the long cooking that does that. Many of the more health conscious recipes call for bones with little or no meat, which makes a less tasty broth. Don't know why you'd wsnt to go to the time and efhort of simmering stock for 14 hours to make something less tasty, but it serms to be part of the trend. I've always thought of broth as good stock with added flavors, for example, chicken stock simmered with a diced carrot for sweetness, a sprig or two of thyme, and enough salt and pepper to make it tasty. The additions are because stock is kept simple, to add savory flavors to foods without already having a distinctive character, other than its rich, meaty goodness. Stock is also rarely salted, because you want to be able to reduce it even further to make sauces, do broth has salt, stock doesn't. Bone broth enthusiasts rave about gelatine and collagen, but those have been components of good stock for centuries, so I don't know why they're suddenly all the rage, other than the fact that these poor people were raised on insipid supermarket stocks that just aren't as rich and flavorful as the real thing. Bone broth is a trend that reintroduces long simmered, yummy broth to people who never had it as children, who never grew up in a house where the smell of roasted bones and aromatics simmering on the back of the stove was a regular part of daily life. Good for them, broth is delicious, it's easy to make, and the newfound popularity makes it easier to find good bones at butcher shops, which had become problematical in some places I've shopped. I can't speak for anyone else, but in my mind, broth is good stock that's been seasoned so it can be served as a clear soup. Why bone broth all of a sudden when it's always been made with bones? Foodie lingo.

Question: Do recipe books from the 1980s still work, or should they be discarded as uselessly outdated?
Answer: How well any recipe book works depends on the book and the cook. Certainly in a world where some people still enjoy experimenting with recipes from Apicius (1st century),The Forme of Cury (1390), and Hannah Glasse's The Art of Cookery Made Plain and Easy (1747) , the 1980s just isn't that far in the past. I still use a recipe book my mom had in her 1960s kitchen, and it works just fine. It does have some less than currently fashionable recipes, and nary a hint of either 70s Nouvelle Cuisine or 90s molten chocolate cake and sun dried tomatoes (no, not together). But it still has some solid comfort food that stands the test of time. Odds are, any cookbook from the 1980s will have something interesting to cook, something that was trendy and now seems passe, and a bunch of stuff in between. The only way to decide if the book is worth keeping is to browse through it, try one or two recipes you think you might like, and make up your mind after you've tasted the results.

Question: Can you cook a pumpkin after you use it for a jack o'Lantern as long as it's still firm?
Answer: The pumpkins used for jack o'lanterns have very little flavor. The best pumpkins for cooking are the much smaller sugar pie pumpkins, the big white French ones, even butternut squash or Japanese kabocha. And unlike many canned fruits, pumpkin puree (not pie filling) is actually very tasty, and a lot less trouble. Also, even if you only use your jack o'lantern for one night, it dries out, and it's exposed to things you don't want in your food.

Question: What is the correct word, "fresh baked bread" or "freshly baked bread"?
Answer: Fresh is an adjective that describes the state of the bread (a noun), so the proper phrase would be fresh bread. If you want to describe how recently the bread was baked, you would use freshly, an adverb that describes the verb baked. Freshly baked bread is grammatically correct in that case.

Question: How do you keep meringue from sticking to paper?
Answer: If you use baking parchment, meringue shouldn't stick to it. If it does, the best way to remove it is to use a very lightly dampened sponge on the back of the parchment. This will enable you to peel the paper from the meringue. In my experience, this happens if you try to bake meringues on a humid day, or if you don't let them dry in the oven after baking.

Question: Can you make all-purpose flour with bread flour?
Answer: You can certainly adjust the gluten content of your bread flour downwards, if you want to do that. There are a number of options for doing this. You can use cornstarch, the way all purpose flour can be changed to cake flour, by removing 1 1/2 tablespoons from one cup (125 grams) of flour and replacing it with the equivalent measure of cornstarch. You might combine your bread flour with a low or no gluten flour, such as millet, barley, brown rice, buckwheat, or oat flour. You can also use things like coconut flour, almond flour, or fine ground cornmeal. Remember that different flours will absorb more or less liquid, and adjust your recipe accordingly. If you are aiming for a specific protein content (AP flour averages about 11%), you will need to do some calculations based on the amount of protein in your bread flour, and the protein in the substitute. If you just want something slightly lower in protein, fiddle with the proportions until you get something that behaves the way you want.

Question: How do you keep your sourdough from being too dense?
Answer: The things that make sourdough or any bread too dense are actually fairly simple. Bread rises well when the dough has a well developed gluten structure, enough hydration to allow full expansion during fermentation, proofing, and baking, surface tension that encourages the loaf to rise up instead of out, and enough time at all stages for the yeast to create CO2, as well as helping develop the gluten and improve flavor. A final method to improve the crumb of your sourdough is proper oven prep, or baking in a cloche or dutch oven. None of these things are complicated in themselves, but learning to recognize when you've done it right takes practice. The biggest problem bakers who are new to sourdough run into is time. Sourdough cultures work more slowly than commercial yeast. It can take hours for a fed sourdough to reach its maximum activity, and more hours for the dough to ferment. You need to cultivate patience, and learn to recognize when your culture is ready and active. Some people recommend a float test, where you drop a small piece of the culture into a bowl of water and see if it floats. I prefer feeding the culture in a straight sided glass container, so I can see when it has doubled. High hydration is another key to lighter, airier breads. Bakers define hydration as the percentage of water in the dough using the total weight of flour as 100%. So a dough made with 1000 grams of flour at 70% hydration would need 700 grams of water. A typical sourdough recipe would call for a 20% inoculation, or 200 grams of fed, active sourdough starter. Many sourdoughs, especially the popular no knead breads, use hydrations in the range of 75% - 80%. These high hydration doughs need some practice to work with, but they are key to those impressive open crumb sourdoughs everyone seems so enamored with these days. Time. Time is the key to proper fermentation and proofing. While bread made with commercial yeast can be fully fermented and ready for shaping in 60-90 minutes, sourdough takes more time. The starter in the picture above takes five hours to double after feeding, at 80°F. Longer in cold weather. The dough made with it takes the same time for a first rise, after three stretch and folds at 30 minute intervals. Then it gets shaped and popped in the fridge for an overnight rise. Basically, a two day process instead of an afternoon of baking. Another key to a good rise is the shaping of the loaf. Developing surface tension as you shape your bread ensures that it will rise well. There are a lot of ways to do this, and dozens of videos by professional and hobby bakers demonstrating their techniques. Once the dough has proofed and is ready to go into the oven, slashing is another way to control and improve the rise. The last thing to think about is baking. There are ways to prepare a home oven to get a better rise. Professional ovens inject steam during the baking process. Home bakers can imitate this in several ways. One is to put a pan of boiling water in the bottom of the oven to create steam, or to spray the sides of your oven with water, close it for 30 seconds, spray it again, then put the bread in to bake. A pizza stone or steel, properly preheated for at least 45 minutes for the stone and slightly less for the steel, provides direct heat on the bottom of the loaf. A simpler method is to bake your bread in a dutch oven or a ceramic cloche. This traps steam, which lets the crust stay moist longer, encouraging it to expand. Both dutch ovens and ceramic cloches need to be thoroughly preheated to do the job. I know. This is a long answer to a simple question. But if you take it one step at a time, you will end up with better bread.

Question: What type of white flour works best for whole wheat bread?
Answer: As a general rule, most whole wheat bread is made with a combination of bread flour and whole wheat flour. Up to 40% whole wheat by weight will give you a loaf that is similar in texture to an all white loaf, only slightly denser. More than that and the whole grain flour begins to weigh down the dough. You can make a 100% whole wheat bread, but you won't get the same light crumb you get with a blended loaf. If you use a blend of bread flour and whole wheat flour, it's a good idea to either make a preferment with the whole wheat flour or to do an extended autolyse (combine the flour and water, then let it sit until the flour is fully hydrated before adding yeast and salt). This softens the sharp edges if the bran, which can slice the gluten chsins, making it harder to get a good rise.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Which ingredients can you add to pizzadough other than flour, water, yeast, olive oil, salt and sugar, to make it taste better?
Answer: Well, I certainly wouldn't add sugar. It's completely unnecessary, and adds nothing to the flavor of the dough. The ingredients you want are flour, water, salt, and yeast, plus time. The secret to really good pizza dough is a rest in the fridge of at least 24 hours, preferably 48, and sometimes as much as 72. The longer the dough has to ferment, the more time the yeast has to work on breaking down large, tasteless molecules into smaller ones we can taste. A long rest also relaxes the gluten, so you don't need olive oil to make the dough more extensible. Any other flavors you want in your pizza are added as toppings, ideally, the simplest, best quality ingredients you can afford. Pizza is definitely one of those foods where less is more.

Question: What is the difference between a chocolate cake and a brownie?
Answer: There's a bit of overlap, as some people enjoy cakey brownies, while others like a dense, moist chocolate cake. But in general, here are a few differences Brownies begin with melted butter and chocolate, while cakes begin with creaming room temperature butter and sugar. Brownies need melted chocolate, while many chocolate cakes are made only with cocoa powder. Most brownies have a higher proportion of eggs to flour than most cakes. Brownies don't include milk or buttermilk, and don't use leavening, unless they are cakey brownies, in which case they will include either baking powder or baking soda. The cake that's most like a brownie is a flourless chocolate cake, which is almost pudding-like in the center, and delicious with fresh berries and whipped cream. As I said at the beginning, all of these distinctions hapoen along a spectrum. Sometimes one person's brownie is another person's cake.

Question: Judging from sitcoms I've seen from the 1950s and 60s, was roast beef and potatoes a very popular main dish for middle class families back in those times?
Answer: The roast beef that showed up on so many sitcoms was more aspirational than actual. Yes, meat and potatoes were a fairly standard offering, but a big roast like that was more likely to be an occasional thing for special dinners. Family gatherings on the weekend or holidays, dinner with the boss, stuff like that. I know that on our table growing up, we were more likely to have less expensive cuts of meat that required braising, not roasting, and lasted for several meals, including sandwiches for school lunches. And we ate a lot of casseroles in between those roast dinners.

Question: When eating an ice cream dish containing a maraschino cherry, do you eat the cherry first, last, or somewhere in between?
Answer: I don't eat maraschino cherries. They have an odd, offputting flavor. I usually offer them to the other people at the table. Now if I get a fresh cherry, I'm definitely eating that first.

Question: How do people eat pizza daily knowing that it is made up of white flour?
Answer: I am 64 years old. In my entire life, growing up in New York City, which is famous for its thin crust pizza, I don't think I've ever met a single person who ate pizza daily. A couple of times a week? Sure. But daily? So let's forget the hyperbole and get straight to the main event. White flour versus what? Whole wheat or other whole grains? White flour versus those depressing and unconvincing cauliflower crusts so beloved of the keto crowd? Or simply no pizza at all, ever? Is white flour bad for you? No. In moderation, it's fine. It isn't as good as whole grain flours, whether of wheat, rye, or other grains, but it isn't actively unhealthy. In fact, most white flour in the United States is enriched with minerals and vitamins, meant to restore some of the nutrients removed with the germ and the bran. And people generally don't use bleached flour to make pizza, they use unbleached bread flour, Italian pizza flour if they're feeling fancy, even locally grown and milled specialty flours, if they're catering to an upscale clientele. Eating pizza every day, with its generous load of carbs and fat, would probably not be a good idea. Eating the occasional slice or two, as part of a healthy, well balanced diet, is fine, even if the crust is made with white flour. And if it really bothers you, there are plenty of recipes out there for whole grain pizza.

Question: A chef on TV was pushing a roller pin on a cold tart dough making wave-like prints. The chef said: “this is the bridging/ridging technique.” What’s the right spelling for this technique?
Answer: It's called ridging. You use it to help make cold pastry more malleable, and to evenly distribute cold butter in things like puff pastry. It's similar to beating cold pie crust with your rolling pin before rolling it out, only more controlled.

Question: How do you get the most flavor out of mint leaves?
Answer: If you're adding them to a drink, you bruise them or muddle them with some sugar. You can also steep them in simple syrup (equal parts sugar and water, cooked until it is clear). Simple syrup is a great way to add flavor to drinks. You can make it with mint, ginger, mixed spices, vanilla beans, cranberries, anyrhing you want, really. And it keeps in the fridge for several weeks.

Question: Can I buy yarn that is already wound into a ball, or do I need to buy a winder?
Answer: Most yarn from large companies comes in center pull skeins or pancakes, so you don't need to wind it into a ball. From the phrasing of the question, you aren't working wirh lots of yarn on big projects, so winding by hand will be fast snd economical. If you end up falling in love with knitting or crocheting, you can then decide to spend money on a swift and ball winder, though the swift is the more useful of the two.

Question: Does the Jewish law that prohibits eating meat with dairy products apply to meat that is grown in a lab?
Answer: The decision is still out on whether lab grown meat is even kosher. Lab grown meat seems problematic, for a number of reasons. One major requirement for processed food to be kosher is that it needs to be produced by Jewish workers, or supervised by Jews as it is produced, in a plant that undergoes periodic inspections to make sure it is following all the procedures to keep it kosher. So only meat produced in a properly certified lab would be acceptable. Something else that occurs to me is the injunction to eat meat only from animals that have cloven hooves and chew their cud. I don't see lab grown meat meeting either requirement, but some rabbis may decide that since the original cells come from kosher animals, then the meat is acceptable. That doesn't mean it will be okay to eat lab grown meat with dairy. It's still meat, and it is forbidden to combine the two. In fact, even though the original injunction doesn't apply to poultry, Jewish people who are serious about keeping kosher don't eat dairy with poultry either. Rabbis feel that if you get into the habit of eating chicken with milk, it might become acceptable to do it with other meats, or lead to practices that combine dairy and meat by mistake. So no, I doubt that lab grown meat will be considered kosher, unless it is produced under very specific conditions. And if it is, it certainly won't be okay to add dairy to the plate. Meat, after all, is still meat, whether it comes from an animal or a laboratory.

Question: What do I do with bad quality cocoa powder? My brother bought a gallon of it but it doesn't dissolve well but I don't really want to waste it.
Answer: The fact that it doesn't dissolve isn't an indicator of quality. Cocoa powder is not really soluble in water. To get it to make a smooth suspension in hot milk or water, the best technique is to mix a little water with the cocoa powder to make a smooth paste, and then stir it into the hot liquid. When you use commercial hot chocolate mixes, they dissolve readily because they are mostly sugar. If your cocoa powder tastes off, that is rancid, rather than bitter, then it's no good and you need to throw it out. Otherwise, it's fine for baking and for making hot chocolate, and there's nothing wrong with it just because it won't dissolve.

Question: My mom refuses to give my kitten pork because “it will give him worms even if it is cooked”. Is this true? Should I still give him pork?
Answer: Are you and your mom eating the pirk? Does ot give you worms? No. So it won't give your kitten eorms either. The broth is important, because cats get most of their water from the food they eat, snd often don't drink enough on their own. Remember that cats require special nutrients that they won't get from table scraps, and consult a vet to determine the best diet for your cat.

Question: Does it matter what temperature the butter is when making a pie crust?
Answer: Yes, it matters. The temperature of the butter affects the texture of the crust. Do you want a light, flaky crust or do you prefer a crumbly, slightly denser version. The temperature of the butter and the amount of very cold water you use makes a big difference, as does the way you incorporate the butter. Cold butter is preferred for flaky crusts, rubbed in with your fingers or ir cut in with a pair of butterknives or a pastry cutter. Lumps of butter should be visible in the flour, because when you roll put the dough, these lumps create pockets of steam, which help the crust separate into layers. If the butter is worked into smaller pieces, as happens in a food processor, you get a different texture, a closer, more crumbly dough. Neither 8s wrong, it's a matter of personal preference. But if you use room temperature butter, the crust will be much denser, hard to cut neatly, snd heavier on the tongue. It just isn't as nice to eat. A good pie crust is one of the more difficult things to master, in the world of pastry. It requires a deft hand. And very cold butter.

Question: Do you cover stuffed peppers when baking?

Question: Why do we need the four ingredients flour, yeast, water, and salt to make bread? What happens if we take out one of them? How is the quantity of each one determined and why?
Answer: Of the four ingredients, only salt is optionsl, and only in certain styles of bread. Tuscany makes a well known bread with no salt, because it is intended to be eaten with salty foods. But without those accompanying flavors, the bread tastes flat. But there are reasons aside from flavor to add salt to bread. While salt can slow down the initial activity of yeast, it also strengthens the gluten structure of the dough. And slowing down yeast csn be a good thing, becsuse the slower the rise, the more flavor you can develop. As for the proportions of each ingredient in a basic bread dough, you want to measure all ingredients as a percentage of the total weight if the flour. This is known as baker's percentages, and it is useful because it lets you scale recipes according to how much bread you're baking, according to how much flour you start with. Bakers use different amounts of water to get different effects, so the first cslculation is the water, which can range from 60% - 65% for a stiff dough, to as much as 85% for a wet dough like ciabatta. This is referred to as hydration, so if someone says they use a high hydration dough, you know they are working at the upper end if the scale. Salt is usually 2% of the flour, and yeast about 1% - 1.2%. So once you weigh your flour, the rest of the ingredients are easy to calculate.

Question: I found a really weak kitten on the street yesterday, I tried giving it water, pulses, legumes, bread crumbs and biscuit but it would neither eat nor drink anything, what can I do to help the little kitten?
Answer: None of those foods are anything a kitten would eat. Cats are obligate carnivores, and kittens need a good diet to grow and be healthy. If the kitten is that weak, it may be sick, or it may have worms that need to be taken care of immediately. Step one is to get the kitten to a vet, as quickly ad possible. Step two is to feed it a proper diet. You don't say how old it is, so you may want to start with kitten milk replacer, then feed it specially formulated wet food for kittens. You cannot feed a cat a vegetarian diet, even if you are vegetarian. It will kill the cat.

Question: How can I make my own floral painting without copying from others?
Answer: I think Lori nailed it on her answer. Instead of looking at other artist's paintings, look at actual flowers. They're everywhere, from the dandelions in your lawn to the exotic blooms at the fancy florists. You can draw them where they grow, you can bring them home and put them in a vase, you can take a single bloom and copy it as realistically as you can, or use the bright mass of a bouquet to inspire an abstract painting. You can draw or paint the flowers in any style you like, from cartoons or anime, to hyperrealism, and everything in-between. The bottom line is simple. If you want to call yourself an artist, sooner or later you must begin making your own work. Copying isn't art.

Question: How do you get the choke out an artichoke before cooking?
Answer: The best tool I've found for this is one of those serrated grapefruit spoons. Cut the top off the artichoke, spread the leaves, and use the sharp edge of the spoon to remove the choke. It's easier to do after the artichokes have been steamed, but if you want to stuff them, you definitely need to remove the choke first.

Question: Are Twinkies very bad as a food? How is the word created to mean bread?
Answer: Twinkies are not bread, they are a snack cake that is synonymous with highly preserved food that lasts forever. They are a light yellow cake with a cloyingly sweet filling. They aren't good for you, being full of sugar and having very little nutrition to compensate for the carb overload. But they probably aren't much worse for you, as an occasional treat, than any other low quality snack. One Twinkie every eight or ten years or so, isn't going to do any harm. Are they bad as food? They're not as tasty as good baked treats, and they have minimal nutrition and lots and lots of empty calories. And they are definitely not bread, they're cake.

Question: Should I do one paper mache layer at a time, one layer of strips then let it dry, or can I just cut up a whole newspaper and apply all the strips at once?
Answer: If the project is large, or the mixture too runny, you will have problems wirh slumping due to the weight of the water. Trust me -- my largest paper mache projects have been over thirty feet long, on frames made with twisted iron rods and chicken wire. Small scale projects can be layered all at once if they have a porous core, and dried by setting them in front of a fan to aid with evaporation. How many layers you apply at a time will depend on the size of the work, how absorbent your paper is, and whether you want a thick, soft layer of pulp to model, or just want to cover a form as cleanly as possible.

Question: How do I make a tassel out of yarn?
Answer: This is how I do it. You can wrap the yarn around anything wide enough to create the length of tassel you want, or you can cut a piece of foamboard or cardboard to an exact measurement. I like to make notches at the side to hold a length of yarn for tying, and notches at the top and bottom to keep the wrapped yarn in place. Then you just wrap the yarn as many times as you like, and tie it tightly at the top before cutting the bottoms of the loops. After that, you take a piece of yarn, tie it around the top of the tassel to secure it neatly, and trim the bottom so it looks neat. If you use a multi-stranded yarn, you can unravel it to make the tassel look fluffier, and you can use contrasting yarn or ribbon for the wrap, for decorative effects.

Question: What should I eat instead of a bun at work (I can't eat gluten)? Gluten-free bun is a bit expensive.
Answer: The answer seems obvious. Eat something other than a bun There are hundreds of gluten free options, ranging from a piece if fresh fruit to a bag of nuts and dried fruit, to gluten free baked goods you can make at home and bring to work (far more cheaply than buying gluten free food in a shop). You can bring a salad, with the dressing in a separate container. You can bring jerky, if you aren't vegetarian, or hard boiled eggs with a bit of salt and pepper in a paper twist. Even potato chips, if you don't object to junk food. The possibilities are endless. All you need is a little imagination and ten minutes of prep time in the evening, to pack your lunch and put it in the fridge.

Question: Wouldn't it be nice to see a restaurant with dental floss on the tables instead of toothpicks? Wouldn't that be fun to watch?

Question: How can one stop bugs from eating paper mache sculptures?
Answer: Traditional paper mache is made with wheat flour. The only way to keep bugs from eating it is to seal the sculpture with several layers of varnish, or to gesso and psint it. There are also more modern formulas using craft glue or an equivalent, which you can find on DIY craft sites. I have used acrylic medium thinned with water, which works fairly well. Since these are made with synthetic adhesives, they are less likely to attract bugs. The objects still need to be sanded and sealed, to preserve the surface, but they won't be buggy.

Question: How do you know if you’ve kneaded whole-wheat dough enough? Is it supposed to be rougher than white bread dough?
Answer: If your dough has a high percentage of whole wheat, more than 25%, it will feel different from an all white wheat dough. The higher the percentage of whole whest, the less likely you are to be able to use a windowpane test. You just need to make the same dough enough times thst you know when it feels right. You should be able to stretch the dough without breaking it, even if it won't be as thin as the typical windowpane test. Some of the roughness of the bran can be eliminated by doing a preferment with the whole grsin flour and a bit more water than ypu would use in an ordinary preferment. This softens the bran, making it easier to develop a good gluten structure. You can also simply extend the initial autolyse with all the flour, agsin using slightly more water, since whole wheat absorbs more water than regular white flour.

Question: I left my Swiss meringue buttercream in my fridge whilst I went out and when I came back, it went a bit stiff, how do I fix this?
Answer: Just take a wooden spoon and beat it until it is smooth and supple. You'll probably want to leave it at room temperature for a while first, because butter sets when it gets cold. Also, if you're going to refrigerate frosting, remember to smooth the plastic wrap directly on the surface, so it doesn't develop a crust.

Question: Is it better to not use refs in drawing? I mean, you're not tracing but you are kinda stealing someone's idea.
Answer: Every artist who does even vaguely representation work uses references at one point or another.The reference could be an object or person, a photo of an object or person, even another artist's rendering of an object or person. Or an animal, of course. You can copy other artist's work because you want to learn from their work. Or you can copy it because you have no idea how to approach a subject. Or you can copy it because you simply have no ideas. Three very different approaches to references. You can also just use a reference as a reference. If you want to draw a pterodactyl, but haven't got a clear idea of how their wings are attached to their bodies, you look at some references, then make a drawing that makes anatomical sense, instead of some beast that doesn't quite work. If you want to draw a dragon, you look at drawings of dragons, and decide whether you want to create a medieval dragon, a Chinese dragon, a wyvern, or a Welsh dragon. Then you take those design ideas, and do your own original interpretation. If you aren't sure how to draw a hand, you either draw from life, or you look at photos and drawings of hands, and practice until you don't need references anymore. What you don't do, ever, is pass someone else's work off as your own. Use it as a jumping off point? Call it an homage, or label it “after such and such, by so and so.” Nothing wrong with that. Artists have been inspiring one another for centuries. But you have to be honest about what you're doing. And at some point, you need to leave the reference behind, and make your own art.

Question: What should I prepare with 10 lbs of fresh pears before they go bad?
Answer: Got some disposable pie tins? Peel and slice the pears, about 1/4″ thick. For each cup of pears, add a tablespoon of cornstarch ot tapioca, the zest and juice of half a lemon, and 1/4 - 1/2 cup of sugar, depending on how sweet the pears are. If you like nutmeg, grate some nutmeg into the mix. Toss everything together, then fill the pie tins right to the top, cover them in plastic wrap, then foil, and freeze them. Anytime you want to bake a pie, you can pop the frozen filling into an unbaked crust, add a top crust, and bake it. Becsuse you’re starting with frozen filling, by the time it's hot and bubbly there's no worry sbout that dreaded soggy bottom. You can also take any recipe for apple sauce or apple butter, and use your pears instead. Both can be frozen and will last for months.

Question: Why is this sculpture worth 91 million dollars? It does have a type of reflection that I've never seen anywhere before. Why are there 2 of them?
Answer: There are actually four copies of Rabbit. Koons had three casts made, plus an artist's proof. Artists often make more than one cast of a piece, numbering them accordingly. As to why a piece by Jeff Koons is worth $91 million, only the buyer can answer that. The value of a given artwork is set by a number of different criteria, among them the fame of the artist, the perceived investment value of the piece, historical interest, personal taste, and the collecting philosophy of the individual or institution. At lesser price ranges, personal taste also enters the equation, but record setting prices like this are all about percieved value and competition. Keff Koons is one of the most recognizable of contemporary artists, his pieces are held in a number of very well known collections, and that adds to the value of other pieces as they come up for auction. Since the value of each work is determined in part by what other works by the same artist have sold for, it becomes a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy. As to why works by Jeff Koons command any price at all, well that's a mystery only the buyers can explain.

Question: Would instant noodles be healthy if you didn't use the seasonings which are included?
Answer: They're instant noodles. They aren't designed to be healthy, they're designed to be a quick, easy meal or snack. With or without the seasoning packet, they won't add much nutrition to your diet. That said, they aren't really unhealthy either, as sn occasional thing. Question: Where can I buy a huge blank canvas to do an oil painting on? I need something the size of a wall in a house.

If you really want to work on a large csnvas, talk to someone at your local art supply shop. They'll be more than happy to sell you the materials, and to explain how to assemble them. For an added fee, most stores will assemble and deliver your canvas.

Question: What did the average American family eat before immigrants from Italy and other countries brought over pizza, pasta, chili, and other food?
Answer: Well, Italian immigrants didn't bring us chili. And there were plenty of immigrants from other countries before the Italians arrived, along with hundreds of Native American tribes, all of whom had their own individual cuisine. There was a large influx of Italian immigrants to the US between 1900 and 1915 -- at approximately 3 million individuals, they were the largest group of immigrants at that time, the majority from southern Italy. They had a decided impact on American cooking. And American ingredients changed the way they made their traditional foods. But they were far from the first group that did that, and American cooking was as varied as the countries its settlers came from. Early American cookbooks have a decided English influence, but food was very regional in those days. There would have been Dutch and German food in the northeast, a burgeoning southern cuisine influenced by both Native American cooking and that of African slaves, and other cuisines brought to the new world by other settlers. The beginning of the twentieth century is actually fairly late in rhe development of American cuisine. An average family would have eaten what was produced in their local area, influenced by their cultural heritage, so its difficult to define exactly what kind of food they would have eaten. But the US had a number of vibrant food cultures long before the influx of Italian immigrants reached its shores.

Question: How do you sew a stuffed animal by hand?
Answer: There are all kinds of patterns for stuffed animals out there. You can use those, or you can design your own. Hexadog, from my own pattern, with button eyes and button joints. Many animals follow a similar pattern, so once you figure out the basic configuration, you can alter the pattern pieces to suit your fancy. A commercial pattern, whether you buy a paper pattern or download one from a craft site, will have step by step instructions for how that particular pattern is assembled. You need to know a few basic stitches, and you need to have some specific supplies. You want strong thread if the toy will get hard use by a child. Quilting thread is good, as is buttonhole thread. You can use buttons for eyes, as in that first image, or you can buy glass eyes in a number of colors snd sizes. Depending on the pattern, you will need embroidery thread and felt for the features like noses, mouths, and ears. You can make concealed joints inside the limbs with special mechanisms, and if you want to get fancy, there are joints designed to make heads that nod up and down. Many of these supplies can be found on sites that sell bear and doll supplies. Plush unicorn with net mane and tail, and button eyes. I made this for my grand niece. There are traditional designs for animals like old fashioned teddy bears that are fun to reproduce, if you have a historical bent. There is also a collection of sock animal patterns you can get from the makers of the Rockford red heel work socks. I'm working my way tgrough the patterns with my grand niece, who so far, has an elephant, a monkey, a kangaroo, a lion, and a cat. They're lots of fun, easy to sew, and they have a lot of character. Rockford sock kitty. Remember that if you're making stuffed animals for children, kids under three cannot have toys with choking hazards like buttons. The features need to be made of felt or fabric, or embroidered. You can even draw them with fabric markers. Stuffed animals are fun. They aren't difficult to sew, as long as you follow the pattern directions. And once you have a few under your belt, you can start to design your own.

Question: What is the best ordinary chocolate to use for cake-pops? Candy melts are expensive where I live. The best option I have is to buy normal eating chocolate. What would good options be? (Galaxy, Milky bar, Lindt etc…)
Answer: If you want to use chocolate to cover the cake pops, then you will need to temper it. That's why candy melts are often recommended. There are at least a couple of ways to temper chocolate, one fairly simple, and one more complicated, but with better results. The easiest method is to melt part of the chocolate, finely chop about 40% of it, then add the chopped chocolate to the melted chocolate. This helps create a crystalline structure in the chocolate so it sets firm. The precise percentages will vary, depending on whether you are using milk or dark chocolate, so it's best to check a few cooking sites, to see what they advise. The cocoa content of dark chocolate will also affect how this works. The complicated methid involves heating the chocolate to a precise temperature, cooling it to a precise temperature, then heating it again. It can be very frustrating. As for using candy bars, instead of couverture chocolate, you may get uneven results, depending on the other ingredients. I would look for the best quality you can find, even if it's a bit pricier.

Question: How long does an open jar of olives last in the fridge?
Answer: Honestly? I can't recall olives ever going bad in my fridge, and I eat a lot of olives. I'm sure I've kept some for at least 12 months, due to losing them behind other containers at the back of a shelf. Olives, especially if they haven't been pitted, are pretty persistent.

Question: What would you do if you find a mermaid/merman in your bathtub one day?
Answer: I suppose I would start by asking its name, then proceed from there. Some questions I'd like amswers to would include: “What the hell are you going in my tub, and how am I supposed to shower with you taking up all the room?” Also, “How long do you intend to stay? If the creature has visible naughty bits, rather than a sexless fishtail, I would ask if it would like a towel or sarong to cover them. It may not care, since life in the ocean most likely obviates the need for clothing, other than as decoration. If female, I would want to know how it keeps those ridiculous seashells in place while swimming. That's always bothered me. I'd also wsnt to ask some very impolite questions about how mermaids/men reproduce. I could finally solve the problem of whether they did it like humans or fish, which I know is a perennial bone of contention among fantasy fans. I've always held out for eggs, and the males hatching them in a pouch, like seahorses, but it would be nice to know for sure. The next step, I suppose, would be to offer it breakfast. I'm pretty sure I have some salmon filets in my freezer. After that, things would proceed according to its needs and intentions. If it wanted to stay, it would need to chip in for rent and groceries. If it wanted to get back to the ocean, I suppose we could rent a van and I could drop it off at the St. Lawrence river. We're rather far from the ocean, here in western New York. Again, how did it find its way to my second floor apartment? And how the f**k am I going to get it down stairs and into the back of a van? Not sure how my cats would react to the appearance of a giant fish/human hybrid. Would they want to cuddle in its lap, or stalk it from room to room? Only time will tell.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: What is liquid nitrogen ice cream?
Answer: It's a dramatic, tricksy way of making ice cream very quickly. It also creates smaller ice crystals in the cream, so the ice cream is a bit smoother than the churned style. The few times I've had it, it seemed as much a performance as a method of preparing food. Basically, the custard used to make ordinary ice cream is churned slowly, in a very cold machine, until it is mostly frozen. The churning prevents large ice crystals from forming, so it is smooth and creamy. You can do it at home with a hand cranked machine, an electric one, even a plastic ball that you fill with ice and toss around with your kids. Or it can be done commercially, and much more efficiently, in large machines that make gallons at a time. Liquid nitrogen in a tank has a temperature of about -210°C/346°F. Poured into a bowl with the ice cream base, it freezes it almost instantly, while giving off plenty of dramatic fog. The first time I had it was at a new shop designed for the purpose. They had five stand mixers set up on a gleaming steel countertop, fed liquid nitrogen in tubes from under the counter. They took each person's order for their preferred flavor and add-ins, put everything in the bowl, turned on the machine, and gave it a blast of liquid nitrogen. Three minutes later, you had ice cream. Was it fun? Sure. Was it great ice cream? Well, I got green tea Kitkats in mine, which I really like. I'm pretty sure they were using a commercial ice cream base - nothing special. And it took longer to get our ice cream than it would have if they were scooping it, because each order had to be made individually, there were only five machines, and the bowls and beaters needed to be washed in between each order. So as a fun after dinner treat, it was interesting, but not interesting enough to justify the extra three bucks for two scoops of ice cream. Some friends and I got together and made it ourselves that summer. We made our custard from scratch, used fresh fruit, and made one large batch, so there was no waiting. What we ended up with was smooth and creamy, more gelato than ice cream, and very yummy. Was it special enough to justify paying for the liquid nitrogen and faffing around with it? Sure. Once. Liquid nitrogen is fun, if you're not an idiot. You can freeze cubes of watermelon in it, then use them to turn your mouth into a fog machine. But using it to make ice cream is just a party trick.

Question: What would happen if a werewolf attacked a mermaid?
Answer: An interesting proposition. It seems environmentally unlikely, what with mermaids being creatures of the ocean and werewolves mainly inhabiting forests or small towns with access to forests, depending on where they are found in their fictional habitats. Mermaids do occasionally perch on rocks to comb their long green hair, but many stories describe werewolves as having ttouble swinming, so unless the rock was close enough to leap to from the shore, the mermaid would seem to be at little risk. Werewolves, of course, are pretty good leapers. Let's say there was such an encounter, the rock was within leaping distance, and the mermaid was too slow to evade the monster's jaws. Will she change into a wolf with the next full moon? Werewolves are subject to lunar cycles, and the ocean’s tides are also subject to the influence of the moon. Would she feel the tug of the land as the full moon rose, or would the tide in her blood protect her? Would she crawl out of the sea to run on four legs and howl at the moon; wear her wolf pelt on land and her shining tail in the ocean? There's something selkie-like in the image, though selkies wear thrir seal pelts in the ocean, and walk as humans on land. Really, with magical, mystical creatures, snything can happen.

Question: Are cake and muffins effectively the same thing in terms of their chemistry?
Answer: Yes, sort of. It depends on what kind of cake you're making. For cakes leavened with baking soda or baking powder, the chemical reaction is the same. Sodium bicarbonate + acid = lift. But while the chemicals are the same, the way the batters are assembled is not, and it makes a difference. Muffins depend on a specific method of combining ingredients. It is so universal, it's referred to as the muffin method. Combine the wet ingredients/combine the dry ingredients/add the dry to the wet, stirring until just combined. It's so well understood by bakers that you don't even need to list the steps. Just write muffin method under your list of ingredients, and that's all she wrote. Some cakes use this method. Some just dump all the ingredients into a bowl, stir them up, and call it a day. But others rely on the creaming method, where sugar and butter are beaten together, creating thousands of tiny air pockets surrounded by fat. These air pockets expand under the influence of the chemical leaveners, creating a light, airy crumb. The longer you cream the butter and sugar, within reason, the lighter your cake will be. And there are other ways of getting cakes to be light and tender. Some cakes have no chemical leaveners at all. Traditional pound cake recipes call for one pound each of flour, eggs, sugar, and butter, beaten for one hour to get air into the batter. I always imagine a couple of well muscled kitchen maids trading off, one beating the batter with a wooden spoon while the other polishes the silver. There are cakes lightened entirely with egg white foams, like angel food cake, so delicate it needs to be cooled upside down so it doesn't collapse. There are yeasted cakes like savarins and babkas and panettone, which use biology instead of chemistry for their rise. So yes, where baking soda or baking powder are involved, the chemical reaction is the same. But when it comes down to how they are put together, muffins and cakes are very different animals.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: If I want to replace classic sugar with raisin puree during baking, what will be the ratio for maintaining sweetness (i.e. 1:2)?
Answer: Honestly, this is something you're going to need to experiment with yourself. In the first place, without knowing the recipe, there's no way to calculate how the change in ingredients will affect the final product. In the second place, although raisins contain a lot of sugar, they will not act like granulated sugar in a recipe, because they are full of moisture. You would need to adjust other wet ingredients in the recipe to compensate, removing some milk or egg whites, or whatever is in the recipe. You need to pull out your recipe file, make a few experiments, and see what happens.

Question: Why are pizza rolls called pizza rolls when they’re squares?
Answer: You know, that's a good question. Most of them are neither squares nor rolls, but sort of pillow shaped, round in the center and flat at the ends, where they have been sealed. Pizza pillows sounds much friendlier, doesn't it?

Question: Is there a way for me to make my soft cookies become hard and crunchy without it melting?
Answer: Aside ftom cooking them an extra two or three minutes, there are a few things you can try. Using egg whites instead of whole eggs will make crisper cookies. Because the whites have no fat and are mostly water, they tend to create crisper cookies. Adding an extra yolk makes cookies richer, because the yolks are fatty. Swapping any brown sugar in the recipe for granulayed sugar will also make them crisp. Brown sugar makes baked goods moist and chewy, because it is more hygroscopic (it attracts water) than white sugar. Using a little corn syrup or a few tablespoons of milk will help cookies spread, and the corn syrup helpa browning, for crisp bottoms. Melted butter instead of creaming room temperature butter can also help the cookies spread. Thinner cookies are often crunchier than thick ones, but it depends on the recipe. You need to experiment with one change at a time, until you get the texture you like.

Question: Why can’t you use the same cutting board and utensils when cutting raw chicken and vegetables if it’s all going to be cooked anyways?
Answer: You can if you cut the vegetables first, without letting raw chicken near the cutting board until you've moved the veggies out of the way. Cutting the meat first is just asking for trouble.
