Question: Can you refill pentel pocket brush pen with winsor & Newton ink? Will it clog?
Answer: Winsor & Newton ink, like most drawing ink, contains shellac. As long as you clean the brush thoroughly after each use, it won't clog, but if you leave the ink in the brush for any appreciable time, the bristles will stick together and ruin the brush.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Why do some jambalaya recipes have me cook/brown the meat and set it aside, and others have me leave the meat in the entire cooking process?
Answer: Usually, when a recipe calls for browning the meat then setting it aside, it doesn't mean set it aside for the entire cooking process. You brown the meat in the pan, rendering the fat and creating a fond (the bits of brown stuck to the bottom of the pan, which are full of flavor). You then pour off any fat you don't need for sauteing the vegetables, or in the case of jambalaya, for making a roux, then sauteing the vegetables, and you add the meat back in to cook with the rest of the ingredients. If you don’t put the meat back in the pot, how are you going to cook it? If your recipe doesn't include the second step, it may just assume you know jambalaya is a braise, and the meat belongs in the pot.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Where did the practice of defacing paintings with mustaches come from?
Answer: The best recorded historical example is a readymade produced by Marcel Duchamp, the daddy of Dadaism. In 1919, he took a postcard of the Mona Lisa, drew a moustache and goatee on the poor girl, and labeled the work L.H.O.O.Q. The letters, pronounced by a native French speaker, sound like a phrase meaning “she's hot in the ass,” describing a woman who is sexually exciteable. Duchamp pioneered the idea of the readymade, taking everyday objects, manipulating them in some minor way, and calling it art. He also had a pet lobster. His upside down urinal, exhibited under the title Fountain, is more well known than L.H.O.O.Q., but people have been drawing moustaches on paintings ever since, so perhaps his enhancement of the Mona Lisa had the more far reaching impact.

Question: What have you made with raisins?
Answer: The simplest thing I make with raisins is a combination of salted nuts and either raisins or apricots. It's a great quick energy snack, and it can be put up in zip top bags so you can stuff one in your bag on the way out the door. I got in the habit of keeping one handy when I had an office mate who would go into a low blood sugar meltdown every afternoon, because she skipped lunch. It kept her from yelling at people. I put raisins in homemade granola, in raisin walnut soda bread, in cinnamon raisin bread, and occasionally in rock cakes, because my supermarket doesn't carry currants. They also go in the poppy seed filling for hamentashen, along with orange juice. Every once in a while, I add them to a bowl of oatmeal or Cheerios. Raisins also make their way into savory dishes. I like them in couscous, combined with almonds or hazelnuts, and in a spicy chicken tagine. Apricots are more traditional, but that's how my grandfather made it, so I stick to his recipe.

Question: Can I use a waterbrush/aqua brush with gouache?
Answer: I think the aquabrush, or similar brushes with nylon points, are best used with transparent media. Gouache has opaque pigment which will most likely not transfer well through the marker-like point. I suggest giving it a try with diluted gouache to see if you like the results, but you'll most likely get better results with a traditional sable watercolor brush

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Do you prefer physical books over e-books? And why?
Answer: I own, and have read, at least 1000 physical books, though I've been eliminating much of my collection because they just take up too much space. I love my books, but they require maintenance. My Kindle library, after ten years of collecting, has something on the order of 2000 books and magazines. I like the convenience of ebooks, the transportability of my entire library in easily accessible form, and the ability to adjust the light and font size on an ebook. I like that an 800 page novel weighs no more than a short novella and can be read with one hand. There are some books I prefer in hard copy. Anything where illustrations are important, like art books and exhibition catalogs, cookbooks, both for illustrations and ease of use, comic books and graphic novels, where the entire page is too small to appreciate on an ereader, but opening individual panels detracts from the appreciation of the overall design of the page. I have paperbacks I've been moving from place to place since college, that are no longer in print, and old favorites I just can't bear to dispose of, despite having a digital copy in addition to the old friend on the shelf. Sometimes you just want to relax with a solid book in your hand, sometimes the ebook is just more convenient. I don't see it as an either/or situation.

Question: What is black pudding called in America?
Answer: Black pudding isn't very common in the US. You usually find it in restaurants that serve British style food. If you asked most Americans, they wouldn't know what it was, and those that do would probably call it blood sausage or black pudding. It just isn't a popular menu item here. You can find it at specialty butcher shops, order it online, or look for a store that specializes in British imports, but you aren't likely to find it st your local supermarket.

Question: Why is the wheat germ endosperm removed from wheat grain leaving only the rest of the wheat grain for the purpose of baking bread?
Answer: There are both practical and cultural reasons for removing the bran and germ from wheat flour. Practically, the bran leaves sharp particles in the flour, which slice the gluten strands, making it more difficult to get a good rise. This can be overcome somewhat with a longer autolyse, a period in which the flour and water are combined without the addition of yeast, allowing the bits of bran to soften while the flour hydrates. The germ is removed because it contains most of the fat in the grain. While it is full of nutrients, the fat will cause flour to go rancid more quickly, unless it is stored properly and used promptly. While modern refrigeration largely eliminates this problem, when people relied on cellars for cold storage, whole grain flours were simply less stable than white. It became a tradition. There is also a cultural preference for fine white bread. This has been true since Roman times, when bolted (sifted) wheat flour was reserved for those who could afford it, and mixed grain breads were eaten by poorer folk. The preference for white bread persisted into the middle ages, with some recipes calling for flour to he bolted five or six times before baking bread, and endured through the French revolution, with aristocrats claiming their delicate digestion couldn't handle whole grain breads, while the bread of the people was a whole grain brick. The desire for white bread as an indicator of socisl status is very persistent, despite doctors warning of it's poor nutrition since at least the 18th century. So we remove the germ and the bran, and eat less healthy bread.

Question: How can a breadmaker make wholemeal bread taste less salty (bread, flavor, salt, and cooking)?
Answer: If you are using baker’s percentages to mix your dough, the salt should be at 2% of the weight of the flour. Some people limit it to 1.5%. Bread dough needs some salt, because it helps the yeast work. You can always weigh the flour in a volume recipe, then calculate the amount of salt needed, but it's far better ro use an inexpensive kitchen scale, and recipes formulated for it's use. If that 2% still tastes too salty, you can reliably calculate a slightly lesser amount, with consistent results every time.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: How can I make bread with rapid rising yeast? I found it to not work as well as regular yeast.
Answer: Rapid rise yeast is designed for use in bread machines. Because it is formulated with enzymes to speed up the process, it doesn't work well for breads that need a second proof, or for recipes where you want a long, slow rise at lower temperatures. That's one of the best ways to develop flavor in lean doughs, but you can't use rapid rise yeast to do it. There is apparently a distinction between quick rise and rapid rise yeasts, and the SAF instant yeast, but exactly what it is, isn't clear. I do know that SAF red can be used for recipes with cold rises, while SAF gold is preferred for sweet doughs, which can be slower to rise. I use SAF Red for all my home baking, and it seems to work just as well as active dry yeast. And according to several articles I found, the active dry yeast, st least the Fleischman’s brand, no longer needs to he proofed separately, because the processing has improved over the years, resulting in fewer dead yeast cells in the encapsulation. My usual process, when I come up against a question like this, is to make side by side recipes, see what results I get, then decide which I like best. So I guess there will be a couple of yeast experiments in the near future.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Do you follow the feeding guidelines on canned cat food? The can says to feed my kitten 2 1/2 5.5 oz cans per day, but when I try my kitten can't finish all his food. The most he can eat is 1 1/2 cans.
Answer: Most cats only eat as much as they need. I have two adult cats, and they each eat one 5.5 oz can of food per day. They also have kibble for free feeding, but they don't eat a lot of it, maybe half a cup between the two of them each day. If the food is available, your kitten will eat as much as it wants. Some cats are smaller than others, and just eat less. Do be sure you are feeding kitten food, as it is formulated for a younger cat's high energy requirements. Most information I've seen advises feeding one ounce of wet food for every pound of body weight per cat. So unless you have a very large kitten, 2 1/2 cans at 5.5 ounces each would feed a pretty big cat.

Question: Is there a word for “unnecessarily large”?
Answer: I've always liked humongous. It has a nice ring to it. Gargantuan might also answer. Either one can be applied with equal effect to steaks, gaudy houses, or egos.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: How do you pay yourself in a non-profit?
Answer: How do you pay yourself in a non-profit? You don't. A properly run not for profit business has a payroll, just like any other business, and pays its employees a salary or hourly wage, according to the type of work they do. A voluntary board sets policy, including hiring practices and salary ranges, usually by approving an annual budget, and hiring a director to oversee operations. The job title and structure may vary according to the type of organization, but in no case can one start a not for profit business and pay themselves, or take money from the budget for personal expenses. Over a twenty-five year career in the non for profit world, I've seen a number of unscrupulous people start not for profit agencies and use them to gain money or build political power bases. Sometimes they get caught. Sometimes, unfortunately, they get away with the most astonishing crap for a long time. But a long time is not forever, and eventually the chickens come home to roost.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is it true that someone can create a sirloin or ribeye steak out of ground beef only?
Answer: With enough artistry and a judicious amount of meat glue (transglutamase) you could certainly create something that looked like a steak. You could even paint it with those nifty grill marks thry put on frozen burgers, to make it look more authentic. But there is no way to get the feel of a piece of meat made from a single cut of muscle gluing a bunch of ground meat into shape. Companies do take unrelated cuts of meat, stick them together with transglutamase, then cut them to make steaks, but they don't use ground meat, and you can usually see the line where two pieces have been joined. These reformed steaks aren't necessarily bad, but they certainly aren't ribeye.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Why do cats need constant attention?
Answer: They don't, actually. Cats sleep between 16 - 18 hours a day. They will ignore you the entire time they are asleep, unless they are asleep on your belly, hip, lap, shoulder, or back, and you have the temerity to change position. When they are awake they need to be fed, watered, played with, cuddled, and chased off the kitchen counter. Anyone who brings a cat into their home just needs to be prepared to deal with the fact that they are curious, affectionate, and independent creatures who like to remind you of their existence at frequent intervals, often in the cutest, most annoying way possible. They're cats. “Must guard the art!”

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: If you were a medieval toddler having dinner with your family, did I refuse to eat peas and throw your spoon like the modern contemporaries, or are the terrible twos and tantrums a modern phenomenon as some would suggest?
Answer: If you were a poor toddler, you probably ate pottage, with field peas mixed with whatever else your family could find to add to the pot. Food would have been too precious to waste, and your parents would have made sure you knew it. You also would probably have been hungry enough to gobble up your field peas (not fresh green peas), instead of losing them in the rush strewn floor. If you were wealthy, odds are you were eating at the table with your parents, in a private dining room, unless there was a feast. You might yave better quality food, and there would probsbly be meat or fish on the table. And you would be instructed in proper manners from an early age, learning not to sully your napkin or chew on your trencher, though toddlers probably took a while to learn this. I doubt you would have been allowed to throw food on the floor, unless you had very indulgent parents.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Why do we have to pay more for shirts with "single needle stitching"?
Answer: Single needle stitching is both more labor intensive, and less prone to raveling. Double needle stitching uses what is essentially a chain stitch. If one loop of the thread breaks, the rest of the seam can readily come undone. Single needle machines use a lock stitch, which is more secure. In most cases, single needle tailoring uses french seams, in which the first seam and the edges of the fabric are hidden inside a second seam. It is neater and less likely to pucker than the double needle stitching, in which both edges of fabric are folded over each other, and stitched down by two needles at once. Think of the prominent sesms on Levi's jeans to visualize this. Essentially, if you are paying extra for single needle stitching, you are paying for the added labor and a slightly neater appearance. And for a bit if extra endurance, so you don't need to restitch your seams.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: How do you make the pastry called elephant ears?
Answer: Elephant eats or palmiers, are extremely easy to make, if you use store bought puff pastry. Preheat your oven to 400°F. Prepare a baking sheet with a piece if parchment paper or a Silpat. Take a sheet of puff pastry, roll it out to about 1/8″ thick, brush it with melted butter, and sprinkle it generously with cinnamon sugar (1/2 tsp cinnamon per cup of granulated sugar, more if you really like cinnamon). Roll the long edges of the dough in to the center so they meet, and turn the dough on its side so you can slice it into half inch thick pieces. Lay them out on your baking sheet, sprinkle a little extra cinnamon sugar on top, and bake for 18 - 20 minutes, until the sugar is nicely caramelized. You can play with them if you like. Add some different spices, dust the tops with sparkling sugar, even roll some finely ground hazelnuts or pecans into the center. Grated orange zest is very nice. If you want to get more complicated, you can try making your own puff pastry. The store bought stuff isn't made with real butter, and it makes a big difference.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Why is it for nutritional facts on the back of foods, they don't specify about the whole bag, but instead put half or a quarter of the bag’s facts?
Answer: The nutrition information, st least in the US, is always specified on a per serving basis, and the label tells you the serving size. Most manufacturers assume their customers understand that. The problems arise when their definition of serving size conflicts with the customer's assumptions. A container you think is a single serving may be two servings, according to their definition. A packet they think is a single serving may make two servings for someone else. So you need to read carefully, and think about the information a bit.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: How can I get pure cinnamon?
Answer: If you're worried about ground cinnamon being adulterated, you can buy cinnamon sticks and grind them yourself, in one of those electric coffee grinders. I have one for coffee, and one for spices. If you're looking for Ceylon cinnamon, also known as ‘true cinnamon,’ you can buy it at any decent spice store, or order it online. It has a milder, slightly citrusy flavor compared to the more common cassia cinnamon.

Question: Are there any other ways a werewolf can transform without ripping or taking off their clothes?
Answer: The only werewolf I know of who can do this is Charles, the romantic lead in Patricia Briggs' Alpha and Omega series. The rest of the werewolves in the series have to take off their clothing to change, but Charles has the advantage of Native American ancestry and personal magic. He can take his clothing with him, and be fully clothed when he transitions back to his human form.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: If a person never eats any kind of meat or fish or poultry, and never eats any kinds of vegetables or fruits, and only lives on pastas, breads, and potatoes, is he still considered to be a "vegetarian"?
Answer: Yes, but he's considered to be a very unhealthy vegetarian, who will have problems with vitamin deficiencies, and may be both anemic and pre-diabetic. An all starch diet is not recommended, for anyone. Also, what is he putting on his bread, pasta, and potatoes. It sounds incredibly boring.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: When a recipe lists an ingredient with an instruction, do you weigh/measure the ingredient before or after the instruction?
Answer: It really depends on the recipe and the ingredient. If a recipe calls for one tablespoon of minced garlic, you need to mince first, measure later. If it calls for one cup of sifted flour, you sift the flour into the cup, and stop when it's full. If it says one cup of flour, sifted, you measure the flour first, then sift it. A cup of diced carrots is a lot more carrot than a cup of carrot chunks. Recipes that use weight instead of volume measurements are much easier to deal with. 100 grams butter is 100 grams if butter, whether its cubed, melted, or room temperature.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is there a recipe for no yeast conchas?
Answer: I've never seen one. Conchas are made with a lightly sweetened yeasted dough, and a sweeter topping made with shortening, powdered sugar, cinnamon or orher flavors. This topping creates the unique decorations on the rolls, which look like seashells and give them their name. Without the combination of a soft yeasted roll and sweet topping, it just isn't a concha. You could use that topping on muffins made with baking soda or baking powder, but they would have a distinctly different texture. Still tasty, but not a concha.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Someone commissioned me for art but won't pay me. What do I do now?
Answer: Step one: gather all your documentation and forward it to Twitch, along with a formal complaint. They actually do take copyright infringements seriously. Step two: Draw up a formal contract that protects your rights to any artwork you create as a commission, including preliminary sketches and all digital content. You will want to include a preliminary payment of between 30% and 50%, a deadline for final payment on delivery, and a limit on the number of revisions included in the price, so you don't end up with twitchy clients who want you to redo your work a dozen times before they are satisfied. Any additional changes can only be made on payment of an agreed upon price, which is included in the contract. If you can afford it, talk to a lawyer about the form of your contract. If you can't, look online for sample contracts. There are a number of them out there that can be adapted for your use. Don't work on a commission piece until you have a signed contract and a payment in hand.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is there now way I can break the rules and paint over a large canvas that has oil paint background? I want to use acrylic and medium.
Answer: The general rule for painting is to put fat over lean. Oil paints are added on top of a layer of acrylic gesso, and richer medium is used over layers of thinner paints, mixed with more turpentine and less linseed oil. There is no reason why you can't break this rule and experiment, if you don't want to create lasting paintings. It represents centuries of professionsl practice, though before the invention of plastics the sealant on the canvas was usually a natural glue, like the rabbit skin glue you can still buy in art supply stores. But if you want to make ephemeral art, and see what happens, art has no rules. You can do anything you want. Most people would scrape off the oil paint if it was still wet, or paint over it with gesso if it was dry. If you've done a heavy impasto, the texture will show through anything you paint over it. You can then do your acrylic painting with no fear of peeling paint. The other option is to remove the canvas from the stretchers and flip it, to create a brand new surface. You can decide for yourself how you want to pprceed.

Name: Beth Goldowitz
Question: Is there a functional difference between slow cooking stew in my slow cooker, and slow cooking it in a big pot set to simmer on my stovetop?
Answer: Either will cook food in the same manner; the difference is in timing and attention. You can leave a slow cooker on low overnight or during the day while you're away ftom the house, something you can't do with a pot on top of the stove. It's very convenient, or at least it was in those far off, pre-lockdown days. On the other hand, if you're doing a slow braise on top of the stove or in the oven, you need to check it occasionally to make sure ingredients don't burn, especially over a burner. On the other hand, you can add ingredients like vegetables at different times, to be sure they don't overcook. I generally prefer to use my dutch oven, in a low (300° - 325°) oven. If I'm in a hurry, I use a pressure cooker. I actually have a braise in the oven right now, a second attempt to replicate a dish from one of my favorite Chinese restaurants. Beef short ribs, in a sticky, tangy, hot sauce, with tiny potatoes. This attempt has a braising liquid that includes orange juice, brown sugar, five spice powder (made it myself, because there wasn't any on the shelf when I went shopping, orange peel, leeks, garlic, chicken stock, and sesame oil. It smells smazing right now, but it still needs another couple of hours in the oven.

Question: Is bread made with yeast vegan?
Answer: Lean breads made only with flour, water, salt and yeast are certainly vegan. But many breads contain other ingredients -- things like milk butter, honey, eggs, and other non-vegan foods. Unless you make your own bread, it's a good idea to read the ingredients carefully, to make sure the bread is consistent with your philosophy.

Question: What is the best alternative to plastic wrap for meats and cheeses? There have been several stories lately about plastic leaching into our food from wraps and containers. How can we avoid it?
Answer: The best substitute I've found are those beeswax impregnated fabric wrappers. They cling to themselves to wrap food snugly, and they are washable and reusable. You can buy them in a package of assorted sizes, so you have several options. Thry are not quite as airtight as plastic wrap, and don't work well for freezing bread, but for everyth8ng else, they're just fine.

Question: Do professionally trained fine art painters still use red, yellow, and blue as the primary colors?
Answer: Most professional psinters develop a preferred palette of colirs to suit their personal style. So while most of them do have red, yellow, and blue on their palette, along with several other colors, some will opt for ultramarine blue, while others may use cobalt blue or another type of blue. The same is true of reds and yellows. Most paint companies produce five or six versions of each, and artists select the ones they like most.

Question: Is it dangerous to not use recipes?
Answer: Dangerous? Not really. If you are new to cooking, recipes provide ideas for cooking techniques, flavor combinations, and ways to use ingredients you arent familiar with. If you want to learn a new style of cuisine, recipes can give even an experienced cook an understanding of the techniques, seasonings, and popular dishes of that cuisine. But once you know some basic cooking techniques, and gave an idea what kind of things you enjoy, recipes become less important, except as reminders of dishes you've enjoyed in the past, or new ways to explore and expand your repertoire. If you know how to cook, doing it without a recipe is no more dangerous than trying to ride your bicycle without the owner's manual in your pocket.
